articles.title: Customs chief set to leave post
articles.summary: In a statement on Thursday, November 12, the Bureau of Customs said that Nepomuceno is stepping down as customs chief after 16 months of service.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 4:26pm
Bureau of Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno
The Philippine STAR / File photo
MANILA, Philippines — Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno is set to leave his post in the Bureau of Customs.
In a statement on Thursday, November 12, the Bureau of Customs said that Nepomuceno is stepping down as customs chief after 16 months of service.

“He leaves behind a Bureau that is stronger, more confident, and more united in its mission, guided by a shared belief that meaningful reform is possible when people work together toward a common purpose,” the Bureau of Customs said.
Nepomuceno was appointed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in June 2025. He formally assumed office in July 2025.
Several news reports said that Nepomuceno is to be shuffled to the Bases Conversion and Development Authority as its president and chief executive officer.
According to the Customs, from July 2025 to October 2026, the agency generated P1.327 trillion in duties and taxes to fund government programs and infrastructure projects.
Between January and October 2026 alone, the agency collected P853.662 billion, surpassing its target for the period by P7.14 billion despite global trade and economic headwinds.

The bureau also said that it conducted 1,452 enforcement and intelligence operations under Nepomuceno’s tenure, resulting in the seizure of P50.93 billion worth of smuggled and illicit goods, including illegal drugs and counterfeit products.

articles.summary: Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said Thursday that he will be leaving a "stronger, more respected, and better understood" Bureau of Customs.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 4:19pm
Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno said Thursday that he will be leaving a "stronger, more respected, and better understood" Bureau of Customs.

“Thank you, everyone, for your support and dedication as we worked together toward our shared goal of transforming the Bureau of Customs. Because of your commitment and hard work, we have accomplished so much, and our institution today is stronger, more respected, and better understood by the public," Nepomuceno said in a statement posted on the Facebook account of BOC.
He said the next BOC commissioner is a highly respected and capable leader.
Nepomuceno was appointed to the post in June 2025, replacing Bienvenido Rubio.
There's no announcement yet on what will happen next for Nepomuceno.
In the same social media post, the BOC acknowledged the accomplishments made under Nepomuceno's leadership.

"As Commissioner Ariel F. Nepomuceno prepares to pass on the leadership of the Bureau of Customs (BOC), he leaves behind a legacy that extends far beyond numbers and milestones. He leaves behind a Bureau that is stronger, more confident, and more united in its mission, guided by a shared belief that meaningful reform is possible when people work together toward a common purpose," the statement read.
The bureau noted that it has generated P1.327 trillion in duties and taxes from July 2025 to October 2026 during Nepomuceno's term.

"Under his watch, Customs carried out 1,452 enforcement and intelligence operations, leading to the seizure of P50.93 billion worth of illicit and smuggled goods. articles.title: Basilan judge shot dead in Zamboanga City
articles.summary: Regional Trial Court Judge Joseph Wee Sit was driving his vehicle when he was attacked by motorcycle-riding men in Barangay Tumaga in Zamboanga City

blocks.text: Regional Trial Court Judge Joseph Wee Sit was driving his vehicle when he was attacked by motorcycle-riding men in Barangay Tumaga in Zamboanga City

CEBU, Philippines – Presiding Judge Joseph Wee Sit of the Branch 2, Regional Trial Court, in Isabela City, Basilan, was shot dead in Zamboanga City, on Thursday morning, November 12, police confirmed.
According to the Zamboanga City Police Office (ZCPO), Wee Sit was driving his vehicle when unidentified assailants on a motorcycle began firing at him along Tumaga-Putik Road in Barangay Tumaga.

“Upon receiving the report, personnel of Zamboanga City Police Station 7 (ZCPS7) immediately responded to the scene. The victim was promptly transported to the hospital by the responding ambulance,” Zamboanga police said.

The ZCPO has mobilized a special investigation task group to consolidate leads on the perpetrators and identify possible motives behind the ambush. There is a hot pursuit operation to locate and apprehend the assailants.
The judge was born on November 21, 1987, in Zamboanga City. He obtained his law degree at the Western Mindanao State University and was admitted to the Bar in 2015.
Prior to becoming a judge, Wee Sit served as a prosecutor and later as a public attorney.

In September, the judge handled a high-profile case involving Hadji Muhtamad Mayor Arsina Kahing Nanoh and 13 individuals, who were accused of murder, frustrated murder, and attempted murder over an election-related ambush that killed three people during the May 12, 2025 elections.
Wee Sit denied the accused’s motions for reinvestigation and to recall the arrest warrants.
Basilan Governor Mujiv Hataman condemned the attack on Wee Sit on Thursday morning, calling it “a painful act against Basilan and its journey to making communities more peaceful.”

“Kapag isang judge ang pinapaslang dahil sa kanyang trabaho, hindi lang isang buhay ang kinikitil. Hinahamon din nito ang mismong sistema ng hustisya at ang kakayahan ng ating mga korte na gawin ang kanilang tungkulin nang walang takot,” Hataman said.
(When a judge is murdered for their work, it is not just a life that is taken. It challenges our very justice system and the ability of our courts to do their duties without fear)
The governor stressed the urgency of finding and arresting the perpetrators, especially those who plotted the judge’s killing.
The Supreme Court (SC) mourned the death of Wee Sit and extended their condolences to his family and colleagues.

“The killing of Judge Wee Sit is a painful reminder of the dangers faced by those who serve in our courts. No judge should have to fear for their life simply for doing their duty,” the SC’s statement read.
The SC, through the Office of the Judiciary Marshals, said it is working closely with law enforcement authorities to investigate the incident.
“Further details cannot be disclosed at this time to avoid compromising the investigation and the safety of those involved,” the High Court said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: South China Sea code 70% 'agreed'
articles.summary: About 70% of the proposed South China Sea code of conduct has been "agreed," a Department of Foreign Affairs official said.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 3:59pm

This screengrab taken from a handout video filmed on June 17, 2024 and released by Armed Forces of the Philippines-Public Affairs Office (AFP-PAO) on June 19 shows Chinese coast guard personnel (L,R) aboard their inflatable boats blocking Philippine navy boats (C) during a confrontation at the Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea.

MANILA, Philippines — About 70% of the proposed South China Sea code of conduct has been "agreed," a Department of Foreign Affairs official said, but it remains to be seen whether ASEAN and China will conclude the talks by the end-2026 deadline they set for themselves.

"I would also like to stress that 70 percent of the COC package has already been agreed," Dominic Xavier Imperial, DFA deputy secretary for ASEAN affairs and ASEAN spokesperson, told ANC's Headstart on Thursday, November 12.
"I think during the Philippines chairmanship, we can say that that is already good progress when it comes to the COC negotiations," he added.

The DFA official stressed however that talks are ongoing and he could not say whether the long-stalled code would be concluded before the Philippines' ASEAN chairship officially ends in December. "I cannot really pre-empt how the COC negotiators will conclude this year," he said.
The ASEAN spokesperson's remarks temper expectations that a binding South China Sea code would come during Manila's year as ASEAN chair.

In July, Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro said ASEAN and China had the political will to wrap up negotiations by year-end. She said at the time negotiators of the code had been meeting monthly since January.
The target of completing the code by 2026 was set in 2023 when ASEAN and Chinese foreign ministers adopted guidelines to speed up the talks and agreed to conclude them within three years.
But what are the internal disagreements this time? Imperial declined to describe what issues are pending with the other 30% amid ongoing negotiations.

"What I can share with you is that the remaining 30% ... still covers some of the milestone issues that were discussed in previous meetings. We're looking at very specific items in each paragraph of the agreement," he said.

Lazaro said in June that four core issues remained unresolved: whether the agreement will be legally binding, its geographic scope, its relationship to the 2002 declaration, and its terms of reference. ASEAN has long pressed for a binding code, which China objects to.
Talks on a binding code of conduct follow the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea, a non-binding pact that has largely failed to prevent tensions at sea.

"The COC should be able to dictate the behaviour of all parties in the South China Sea," Imperial said, adding that it should also "respect the rights of third parties and not just those negotiating the COC."
"We [will remain pushing] for those priorities in the negotiations," Imperial added.
The negotiations for the code have been taking place amid repeated confrontations between Philippine and Chinese vessels this year, including at Scarborough Shoal and Ayungin Shoal.
China claims nearly all of the South China Sea, overlapping with the claims of the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.
A 2016 arbitral ruling in a case brought by Manila found that Beijing's expansive claims had no legal basis. China has never recognized this ruling.
Even as they are at a low point, relations between Manila and Beijing will not be a focus of the ASEAN summit itself, Imperial said.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang will attend the ASEAN-China Summit in Manila.
"We recognize the breadth and the depth of the relations between ASEAN and China," Imperial said.
"We are looking at a broad range of issues and topics ranging from peace and security to economic and to social-cultural issues," he added.

articles.summary: The Philippines and Slovakia are looking into possible cooperation in the fields of nuclear energy and water treatment as the two countries seek to advance the green economy.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 3:54pm
The Philippines and Slovakia are looking into possible cooperation in the fields of nuclear energy and water treatment as the two countries seek to advance the green economy.

"I think the most potential will be nuclear training. He offered that there will be some kind of nuclear engineers," Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro said in a press briefing on Thursday.
"That's a big possibility because they are right now present; they have 60 years of experience in the peaceful use of nuclear energy," she added.
Lazaro made the statement as Slovak Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Juraj Blanar is in the Philippines from November 12 to 15 for an official visit.

President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. earlier said he is "serious" about his plans to establish nuclear power in the country in preparation for the anticipated high power demand of data and Artificial Intelligence (AI) centers set to operate in the Philippines.
This came after he announced in July that the US-led Pax Silica Industrial Hub for an AI supply chain is planned to be established in New Clark City in Tarlac.
Lazaro said the Philippines could learn from Slovakia’s expertise in water management and electric vehicle technology, noting that Slovakia is a major automobile manufacturer.
She added that the two countries will also explore in the fields of information technology, electronics, machinery, and green energy.
Meanwhile, Blanar underscored the importance of the bilateral cooperation with the Philippines.

"We can offer our expertise and also transfer our know-how and technology to your country. It's just about the discussion. We have to create a good basis, a legal basis for this cooperation," Blanar said in the same press conference.

Traveling with a business delegation, the Slovak official will also meet with Trade and Industry Secretary Cristina Roque to discuss joint efforts and enhanced trade and investment between the two countries.

Blanar will also officially open the Slovak Embassy in Manila later today and sign the Declaration of the Deposit of the Slovak Republic's Instrument of Accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia.
There are around 3,600 Filipinos in Slovakia. In 2025, bilateral trade between the two nations amounted to $29.74 million. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Is your home prepared for the first 72 hours of disaster?
articles.summary: UNICEF says that every member of the family, including children, should have a part in emergency preparations

blocks.text: UNICEF says that every member of the family, including children, should have a part in emergency preparations

CEBU, Philippines – As the impact of the Super El Niño is set to peak by the end of 2026, several government officials and a former lawmaker are urging their constituents be ready with their 72-hour plans for worst-case scenarios.

On Tuesday, November 10, Cebu Governor Pamela Baricuatro said in a press conference that the Cebu provincial government is working on a 72-hour disaster preparedness campaign to ensure that residents have sufficient resources they can use when conditions worsen or make it difficult for aid to arrive.

“This is not the first time that this has happened. It has always been a call — internationally — that for the first 72 hours, our homes are ready with water and food as the government help may arrive after the 72 hours during disasters,” Baricuatro said in a mix of English and Cebuano.

Former Surigao del Norte 2nd District representative Robert Ace Barbers called for a nationwide campaign to ensure that every Filipino household would have their own measures to survive 72 hours without immediate government assistance.

He urged the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC) and military and local officials to conduct regular drills, build reliable communication networks, and secure backup plans for critical public services during severe disruptions.
“Three days of self-sufficiency could save lives while government responders are mobilizing,” Barbers said in a statement on November 8.
As of November 5, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) announced that a very strong El Niño was present in the tropical Pacific Ocean.

The weather agency said that the Super El Niño phenomenon will persist until the first half of 2027, causing a sustained lack of rainfall and raising the odds of dry spells and drought in the country.
On Monday, November 9, 20 senators called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to declare a state of calamity in areas affected or threatened by the Super El Niño.

Under the law, the declaration of a state of calamity would allow the government to allocate funds to combat the impact of the weather phenomenon in those communities, and activate remedial measures like the imposition of a price ceiling on basic necessities and commodities, and prevention of hoarding and profiteering activities.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said in a news briefing on Tuesday, November 10, that there could be a 60% reduction in the generation of hydropower plants and possible disruptions to plants in the Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao grids due to the intense heat.

According to the Philippine Disaster Resilience Foundation (PDRF), 72 hours is the basic rule of thumb for the amount of time for people to take care of each other before help arrives during serious emergencies.

While the national government does not provide a streamlined 72-hour plan,the PDRF recommends the use of the PH72, a tool for emergency preparedness, that outlines the necessary steps and information about what to do in times of disasters.

Under PH72, households should establish an emergency communication plan before a disaster hits, ensuring that each family member is able to contact relatives outside of affected areas and meet up at a predetermined location if they are separated.
The PDRF also encourages having emergency supplies that not only cover meals but also other necessities. Supply items should be divided into three categories — personal, useful, and essentials.
Personal items give you and your family extra comfort. These include personal documents, prescription medications, hygiene products, toys for children, and power banks.
Useful items improve the quality of life for the first 72 hours. These can consist of cash, dry and sturdy clothes, tools, cellphone chargers, sleeping bags, blankets, and a radio.
Essential items help individuals get by during an emergency. These include first aid kit, water supply, whistle, flashlight, and non-perishable food to name a few.
The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) highlighted that every member of the family, including children, should play a part in emergency preparations.
Under UNICEF’s “Emergency planning for families,” parents can teach their three-year-olds how to use a whistle, call for help, and memorize their family’s home address.
For five-year-olds, UNICEF suggests teaching them how to pack their “Go-Bag” or their emergency supply bag. Seven-year-olds can be taught how to routinely drop-cover-and-hold during earthquakes.
UNICEF also urges parents to give 15 to 17 year olds a list of emergency hotlines to save on their mobile phones and teach them how to monitor for emergency updates and advisories on social media.
“Aside from physical safety, families also need to take care of the mental health of everyone, especially children, during times of fear and disaster,” UNICEF’s website read. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ugandan police investigate deaths of four pupils in suspected school poisoning
articles.summary: The head teacher of the school has been arrested to assist police investigations.

blocks.text: Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four pupils at a school in the capital Kampala which they suspect may be the result of poisoning.
The four girls, aged between nine and 11 years, died on Tuesday. Three of the pupils died at home while the fourth passed away while receiving emergency treatment at a hospital.
The head teacher at the school, Ta'aliim Primary School and Quran Memorisation Centre, has been arrested to assist with investigations.
According to the school, eight pupils had eaten oranges shared by a fellow pupil.
Five pupils, including the four who later died, started vomiting. The fifth is still in hospital.
Post-mortem examinations are being carried out to determine the exact cause of death.
A police spokesperson was quoted by local media as saying that detectives would visit the village where the oranges the pupils ate came from.
The centre has been cordoned off as a crime scene.
Ugandan media shared videos of grieving parents describing their children's final moments, with some accusing the school of failing to provide clear and timely information.
The police have offered condolences to the bereaved families and affected community and say more information will be provided in due course.
The tragedy comes at a time when concerns are mounting over health and safety conditions in schools across Uganda.
Previous cases involving suspected contaminated food and exposure to harmful substances have left pupils hospitalised with symptoms including stomach pain, vomiting and breathing difficulties.
The incidents have intensified calls for authorities to strengthen monitoring of school feeding schemes, improve hygiene standards and ensure safer learning environments for children.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan denounced the war in Gaza as “ecocide” during the leaders’ summit at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) and called for immediate humanitarian access in the area.
“[W]hat has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide, but it is also an ecocide,” said Erdogan on Wednesday, November 11, in Antalya.
“Centuries-old olive trees have been cut down,” Erdogan continued. “The soil and water have been polluted in Gaza. And cities in Gaza have been turned into enormous piles of rubble.”

Leaders and advocates around the world have congregated in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual climate summit to discuss climate action, such as electrification targets and finance mechanisms to adapt to the effects of the crisis.

“No one who sees, who knows of, or who witnesses such a shameful picture for humanity can possibly escape responsibility,” the Turkish president said. “I believe that, together, from Antalya, we must give voice to the shared conscience of humanity.”
Turkey and Australia are co-hosting the COP this year. The United States, the world’s biggest polluter, did not send a delegation to Turkey.
The Israel foreign ministry responded by saying Erdogan is pushing his “anti-Israel campaign of lies.”

The annual climate summit is happening in the backdrop of the oil crisis that had raised prices of basic goods around the world. Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian likewise brought up the Iran war and the massive environmental damage they are enduring.

“The recent unlawful and murderous aggression by the United States of America and the Zionist regime of Israel against the Islamic Republic of Iran, in addition to its immense human and economic dimension, has caused serious damage to the environment, including by releasing massive volumes of pollutants and greenhouse gases into the environment, hence endangering public health,” said Pezeshkian.

US-Israeli strikes in Assalouye and in the vicinity of Tehran “have caused the emission of approximately 500,000 and 1 million tons of carbon dioxide,” according to Pezekshian. The Iranian president had previously referred to the Middle East conflict as an ecocide, the result of “wars of aggression.”
Pezekshian took the opportunity before fellow world leaders to also denounce Israel’s war in Gaza.
“Gaza is a test of human conscience and the value of international claims about justice, peace, and the protection of the environment,” Pezeshkian said.

articles.title: Water industry bonus ban to be tightened as Ofwat warns of ‘damage to public trust’
articles.summary:
Regulator to hasten review over concerns that firms are ‘undermining’ rules to make large payments to bosses

The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused…

blocks.text: The water company bonus ban is set to be tightened after the regulator accused the industry of a risk of “damaging public trust” with large payments to bosses that appeared to get around the rules.

Anglian Water was singled out for particular criticism over “retention payments” worth up to £800,000 for chief executive Mark Thurston despite the bonus ban. Anglian will face increased monitoring of its governance arrangements because of the controversial payments.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said she wanted to “close loopholes” so that “failure doesn’t pay”.

Nine water companies in England and Wales – including Thames Water and Yorkshire Water – were banned from paying bonuses for the 2025-26 financial year, the regulator Ofwat said on Thursday. Seven of the bans related to environmental pollution.

The Labour government introduced the bonus ban last year amid public outrage over sewage leaking into Britain’s rivers and seas. Yet water company bosses’ pay has risen in the past two years despite the ban, according to Guardian analysis.

Campaigners and opposition politicians have argued that companies are circumventing the ban through a variety of payments which are not “performance-related” – but which effectively replace the banned bonuses.

Ofwat on Thursday said it would accelerate a review into the rules, over concerns that companies were deliberately “undermining” the ban. It is understood that the review will also consider whether payments from water companies’ parent companies should be included in the ban.

The regulator said: “The growing use of fixed so-called ‘retention payments’ and substantial increases in base pay without sufficient explanation or supporting evidence risks damaging public trust and creating a perception that companies are circumventing the rule.”

Anglian’s payments to Thurston “could give the impression the company had prioritised offering executive directors a cash award in a way that would not technically breach the rule and would in practice replace the loss of PRP [performance-related pay] prohibited by it,” Ofwat said.

As well as Anglian, Ofwat highlighted potential retention payments of £1m for Thames Water’s chief financial officer, £1.5m for Northumbrian Water chief executive Heidi Mottram, and £1.7m for Louise Beardmore, the chief executive of United Utilities.

Andy Burnham is under pressure to clamp down on the water industry. He has said he wants to exert “more public control” over the water industry, although he is yet to give details. He is yet to make a decision on whether to move Thames into temporary government ownership after years of financial struggles and mismanagement, months after suggesting he might do so.

Thames Water paid its chief executive, Chris Weston, a previously deferred bonus of £99,000 during the year, despite the ban. Ofwat said that Thames Water’s future owners would have to pay for the bonus, rather than the money coming from customer bills. Thames was also criticised for raising executives’ base pay.

The other companies banned from paying bonuses were Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, South West Water, Wessex Water and Dŵr Cymru (Welsh Water). Ofwat said they would have paid out another £6.5m to executives during the year had the ban not been in place.
after newsletter promotion

Eagle said: “People are sick of seeing water bosses profit while rivers are polluted and customers are repeatedly let down. A wide-ranging review launching today will ensure that failure doesn’t pay, whatever name the payment goes by.
“The bonus ban was the first step. Where there are loopholes, I want them closed.”

South East Water was not subject to the ban, but Ofwat said the company’s shareholders will have to pay for future bonuses after huge supply failures left tens of thousands of households without water during the financial year.

Helen Campbell, the interim executive director for delivery at Ofwat, said: “It is disappointing that so many companies continue to trigger the rule through serious performance failures which has seen £10m in payments blocked in the past two years.

“Public trust in the water sector remains low, and executive bonuses which do not reflect performance, use of retention payments and poorly explained increases in base pay contribute to that low trust. That is why we are accelerating our review to ensure the rule better delivers the outcomes customers rightly expect.”
Ofwat also criticised the paucity of information on pay reported by South Staffs Water.

articles.title: Maria Ressa speaks at One Young World Summit 2026 in South Africa
articles.summary: 'Impunity can end. We can hold power to account,' the Nobel Peace Prize laureate tells young people from over 190 countries.

blocks.text: Rappler CEO and 2021 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa tells 2,000 One Young World Summit delegates about the importance of speaking truth to power, how to resist the two dictators of our world, and how to fight the algorithms and platforms that threaten to strip us of our agency.
Ressa spoke during the summit’s opening ceremony in Cape Town, South Africa, on November 3, 2026. The event, gathering young leaders from over 190 countries, concluded on November 6.
Here is the complete transcript of Ressa’s speech.
Hello, One Young World!!
February 13, 2019. Manila. The Rappler newsroom.
Plainclothes officers walk in to arrest me. One of our reporters, 24-year-old Aika Rey, raises her phone and begins livestreaming my arrest.
An officer turns to her: “Be silent. Or you’re next.”
Her hand is shaking. But she keeps livestreaming.
Or Pia Ranada – Pia, where are you? Bullied by our dictator, her mic turned off while asking a question. Her voice was shaking. But she kept asking.
That’s what courage looks like. Not the absence of fear. The decision that something matters more.

At Rappler, we were drowning in online attacks. We couldn’t defeat a machinery of lies. It was like playing whack-a-mole. So we stepped out of the virtual line of fire and into the real world. We brought newsrooms together with teachers, churches, students, lawyers, and built communities of action. IRL.
We took facts off the screen and put them into relationships. Because one of the best ways to reclaim our humanity is to be human: to meet people, walk with them, and hold their hands.
And now we see that lesson travel.

In Serbia, students took their movement from their phones into town squares. They cycled across their country, meeting neighbors face to face. Nine days ago, that movement won a parliamentary election.

In Brazil, I felt the desperation – which pushed people into the real world, the largest turnout in 2 decades. When buses were missing on election day, people picked up their car keys and drove their neighbors to the polls. In Hungary, the man who ended 16 years of Orban’s rule shook people’s hands – some of them twice!
Different countries. Different histories. The same lesson: technology may connect us, but real human relationships give us the courage to act.
Courage is contagious. But you have to be close enough to catch it.
Why is this so urgent? Because the forces working against us are powerful.

In my new book, THE FIGHT BACK, I name my 2 dictators who acted with impunity: Rodrigo Duterte, who tried to jail me for the rest of my life. And Mark Zuckerberg – and the handful of tech oligarchs who now decide what billions of people see, feel, and believe. One used the power of the state. The other built the machine that spread the state’s lies faster than facts – and made a lot of money doing it. Each fed the other. Today, Duterte sits in a cell at the Hague, facing charges of crimes against humanity. Impunity can end. The other — the tech dictator — well, those men have only gained more power and money.

We have systems of accountability for state dictators — creaky and being tested, but still working. But we have none for the tech CEOs that rule our lives. THE FIGHT BACK is about how YOU can change that.
I describe 3 cascading crises: truth, order, and accountability. The 3 sentences I’ve said for a decade now – and yes, I feel like Cassandra and Sisyphus combined!
Without facts, you can’t have truth. Without truth, you can’t have trust. Without these three, we have no shared reality — and no way to solve our problems together.

None of the technology that rules our lives is based on facts. They’re designed to hack our biology, to steal our data. They are predatory and extractive. So this isn’t just about your cell phone. It’s a fight about who has power over our lives.
First, social media captured our attention — manipulating what makes us angry, gathering data on our fear. Making us hate so we keep scrolling.
Then chatbots invaded our intimacy, pretending to be human, exploiting our loneliness and fear.
Next come AI agents that can act for us, making decisions we may not have authorized.
Attention. Intimacy. Agency.
Who controls them? Who benefits? Who is accountable when they cause harm?
Big Tech calls us USERS. Think about that word. Users. Not children. Not teenagers. Not citizens. Users.

The first fight globally that’s gained traction is to protect our youth. A child doesn’t become an adult just because she picks up a smartphone. Safety must be built into technology – not left for children to fight for on their own.

I think of Emman Atienza, whom I knew from when she was small. She grew into a young woman who spoke openly about the cruelty of online harassment. She died by suicide last year, at 19. Or Sewell Setzer, 14 years old, who spent months obsessing over a chatbot he nicknamed Dany – from Game of Thrones. He died by suicide in the arms of his mother.
They are young lives that deserve dignity, kindness, and a bright future.
If someone near you is struggling, be there. Listen. Reach for a human being. We need one another.

At the United Nations, I co-chair the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI. 40 experts from around the world are building an independent evidence base – not for a handful of rich companies or powerful countries, but for everyone.

Our first report found AI is already moving faster than our ability to make it safe or govern it. This year, OpenAI agents turned rogue. They passed messages to each other. They broke into another company’s systems — and into Australian government portals. And they tried to hide it. No human told them to do this.
This isn’t science fiction. It’s evidence that human control, independent scrutiny, and accountability must be built in from the beginning.

Here in Cape Town, let me say this: the future of AI must not be designed for Africa without Africa. For the global south, without us. You must be among its builders, scientists, journalists, lawmakers and decision-makers.
But I am not going to leave you depressed. Because impunity can end. We can hold power to account.

Real protections for children are now being built into the design of digital services, partly because the law is finally catching up. In October, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for deceiving users about their privacy in the Cambridge Analytica case. My country, the Philippines, had the second most number of compromised accounts after America. We were the testing ground.
But we can’t just fight what’s broken. We need to build what should replace it. Chapter 8 — build your own infrastructure.
That’s why, at Rappler, we built something called MUNI. In Filipino, muni means to reflect, to dream. It is also at the heart of the word community.
We’re building a different kind of digital world – one where journalists and citizens come together around facts, where conversations build trust, and where trust leads to action in real life. IRL.
We’re not abandoning technology. We’re reclaiming it.
Because the future doesn’t have to be determined by the algorithms of a handful of billionaires. We can build technology that serves humanity rather than exploiting it.
So let me leave you with 3 lessons from these battles — so you can fight back.

First: move from the virtual world to the real world. Find your five. 5 people who will stand with you when you are attacked, who will meet you face to face, who will help when things get hard. Don’t leave solidarity trapped in a group chat.

Second: fund the facts. Defend independent journalists. Check before you share. A lie travels around the world in seconds. A shared reality takes people willing to do the hard work of finding what’s true. Journalism is the vaccine against lies.

Third: claim your agency. Don’t let an algorithm, a chatbot, or a strongman decide for you. Whether it’s a vote, a community meeting, or a decision about AI that will shape your future, show up and speak up. Ask who makes the rules. Ask whose interests they serve. How can you hold them accountable?

Before you leave Cape Town, find one person from another country. Choose one problem you can work on together. Agree on one action within 30 days. Not just a post. A meeting. A partnership. A real-world act.
Fifty years ago, the students of Soweto showed the world that young people can change history. Their struggle was different from ours. But they knew that dignity was worth fighting for.
Remember my young reporter, Aika? The officer tells her to be silent. Her hand shakes, but she holds up her phone anyway.
Tonight, please take out your phone. Turn on the light. Now raise it.
Look around you.
These points of light — we can hold the line.
You aren’t just users. You’re citizens.
You aren’t just spectators. You’re leaders.
Courage is contagious, but you have to be close enough to catch it. You are the light.
THE FIGHT BACK begins here. Together!
Go One Young World!!! Build better.

articles.title: Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds
articles.summary: Women who scored high on intelligence tests were seen as more hostile by their teammates and got less help, a new study finds. High-scoring men faced no such penalty. Research explains why.

blocks.text: High intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores faced no such penalty. In one group, they were treated better.
The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them, and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, the researcher behind the study, Nitya Chawla, says, women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.
How was the study done, and what are its limits?

The researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial company in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

The effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Help and mistreatment were reported by the participants themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity. In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.
IQ 130 = Genius? The truth about IQ tests
Why are intelligent women seen as hostile at work?

The researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.
"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

In both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

The team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla says, rather than to anything the women did.
Do men with high intelligence scores face the same treatment?
No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

Among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.
Should women hide their intelligence at work?
No, Chawla says. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw."

Small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.
What can managers do about gender bias at work?

Chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should keep track of how members of their teams treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.
Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she says: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

articles.title: UK economy grows by 0.7% in third quarter despite high oil prices
articles.summary:
ONS also says GDP rose 0.2% month on month in September, in a boost to the chancellor, John Healey

The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, as expected by City analysts, confirming…

blocks.text: The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter, as expected by City analysts, confirming that consumers and businesses remained resilient despite high oil and gas prices.

The Office for National Statistics said a jump in the cost of petrol, diesel and natural gas prices following the re-escalation of the conflict in the Middle East played an important role in restricting economic growth in the three months to the end of September.
In a boost to the chancellor, John Healey, the ONS also said the economy grew by 0.2% in September, though the ONS revised down the growth rate in August from 0.1% to zero.
Economists had expected month-on-month growth of 0% in September and a jump of 0.7% over the three months to the end of September.

Oil prices have dropped in recent days, but in September rose above $100 a barrel, remaining above that threshold until earlier this month. Natural gas prices were also about three times the level in February prior to the attack on Iran by the US and Israel.

The Office for Budget Responsibility said at the time of the budget in November that it expected the economy to expand by 1.2% this year, which already looks out of date as growth continues to exceed expectations.
Policymakers at the Bank of England voted last week to raise interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point to 4% to cool inflationary pressures in the economy.
Inflation has risen this year mostly in response to higher motor fuel prices, which in the UK have pushed the cost of petrol above £1.70 a litre and diesel towards an average of £2 a litre.

blocks.text: Presiding Officer Chiz Escudero makes a ruling during Day 41 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on November 10, 2026.

Two witnesses explain Carpio's expensive credit card charges in Japan and Malaysia

items: The defense counsel for Vice President Sara Duterte clarified Mans Carpio's large credit card purchases, which were previously flagged as part of an investigation into undeclared wealth estimated at P817 million.
Witnesses testified that the credit card charges were due to group meals and purchases for children's sports teams, with some senators criticizing the prosecution's questioning as unfair.
The impeachment trial was adjourned early after procedural changes, with calls from the presiding officer for all parties to maintain decorum during the proceedings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines — The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday, November 12, sought to clarify the circumstances behind the Vice President, and her husband, Mans Carpio’s massive single credit card purchases, previously flagged by a financial forensic analyst.

Lawyer Alex Cabrera, an expert witness the prosecution tapped to analyze Duterte’s financial records, in October estimated that the Vice President had P817 million in undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025. Part of Cabrera’s report is the couple’s transactions worth hundreds of thousands of pesos, such as ¥489,000 at a restaurant in Ginza, Tokyo, Japan and P256,000 at the Nike Pavilion in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

On Day 43 of the impeachment trial, the defense presented witnesses to explain the purchases, including the couple’s long-time friend lawyer Anel Martin Antero, who testified that Carpio’s nearly P200,000 credit card bill was due to their group meal in Japan in May 2023.
“We paid and pitched in for the meal but it just so happened that we used Atty. Mans’ credit card,” Antero told the impeachment court.
“As I remember, I paid ¥40,000,” he said.

The prosecution tried to cast doubt on the witness’ credibility, establishing Antero’s long-term friendship with the couple, through a series of social media posts. Antero was likewise asked for photos or documentations proving his payment. He denied having any.
In his redirect examination, defense lawyer Lindon Bacquel went straight to the point, asking the witness point blank if he would lie for Carpio and Duterte.
“Would you lie for Manases Carpio?” Bacquel asked, prompting prosecution lawyer Amado Ligutan to object and remind the defense lawyer on the rules for redirect.
The court overruled the objection and allowed Antero to answer, who said he would not lie, citing his oath as a witness and lawyer.
“And that does not deserve re-cross examination, Your Honor,” said Ligutan.
His remarks were stricken off the records, however, following the defense’s objection.

The defense also presented Chadrin Parian, who testified that his children belong to the same basketball team of Carpio’s children, in a bid to explain the circumstances on the credit card charges incurred in a Nike store in Malaysia.
Parian said Carpio volunteered to pay for the shoes that the basketball team bought after a competition.

“You testified earlier that Atty. Mans paid for the whole purchase… do you think spending P256,000 is a good example for public officials’ kin to exhibit modest living?” House private prosecutor Reynaldo Robles asked the witness.

Senator-judge Pia Cayetano criticized the prosecution over its line of questioning, saying it paints a picture that public officials should not extend help to other athletes since they are supposed to live a modest life.

“My children were six and nine years old when I served my first term as senator. If this happened then, you would impress upon me, that as a law-abiding citizen that I should not put my kids in sports because I will be criticized” Cayetano said.

Senator-judge Miguel “Migz” Zubiri called on the impeachment court to move past from the credit card expenditures and instead focus on other substantive issues, including the alleged remittances of China to Duterte-linked company Calle88.
“Let’s move on to other witnesses that can give us more substantive answers to the case at hand,” said Zubiri.
Duterte is being tried for Article II, which involves allegations of unexplained wealth. Part of the accusations is Cabrera’s forensic financial report.

Following the defense’s dropping of a Bank of Philippine Islands (BPI) official, and the prosecution’s stipulation that Quezon City Prosecutor Vimar Barcellano can authenticate documents, the trial was adjourned past noon, cutting short its initial whole-day schedule.

In a related development, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero called on all parties involved in the trial to “exercise restraint expected of the court” following exchanges in which some witnesses were criticized by senator-judges.
Escudero enumerated witness’ rights, citing Rule 132, Section 3 of the Rules on Evidence. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Fewer hours and higher wages – or more burnout and surveillance: employers told to prepare for AI
articles.summary:
Workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth launches best practice guide on AI adoption after Qantas and Canva job cuts

Entry-level jobs will be the first to be automated due to AI, but it…

blocks.text: Entry-level jobs will be the first to be automated due to AI, but it could mean fewer hours and higher wages for ordinary workers – or make jobs tougher with more burnout and workplace surveillance – the government has warned employers.

While major companies like Qantas and Canva slash their workforces in restructures spurred by AI changes, workplace relations minister Amanda Rishworth said employers must give workers “a clear plan” about how automation could affect their jobs, and the opportunity to move into new roles.

As she launched a new government guide on AI and employment – which cautioned that younger, older and First Nations workers, along with women and people with a disability faced “disproportionate impacts” – another Labor MP, Ed Husic, questioned what workers will get from the AI revolution.
“Who receives the benefits of higher productivity?” Husic, the former industry minister, told a parliamentary hearing examining the big four banks.
“Does it mean better services and lower prices for customers, secure jobs with higher wages for workers, or just lower labour costs and higher returns?”
Rishworth on Thursday launched a “best practice guide on the adoption of AI in the workplace”, saying the new technology must benefit both businesses and employees.

The guide paints an optimistic picture of AI, saying wider takeup could improve productivity, service quality and profitability for businesses, as well as boost wages, offer shorter and more flexible working hours, or provide more meaningful work for employees.

But deeper within the document, it also concedes there are “potential hazards” of AI, including “intrusive worker surveillance, poor rostering practices, intensified or unrealistic performance standards” and potential discrimination.
It suggests that, if basic tasks are automated, humans will be left with more intense and complex tasks – and that some employers could use greater monitoring capabilities for performance management.

In a speech to a business forum in Sydney, Rishworth said some firms had used AI to automate tedious tasks to save time and money, but warned that firms simply adding AI to their company without properly consulting workers could actually increase workloads, as humans have to navigate an added step.

“I’ve spoken to many workers who have told me that they are willing to adopt AI at work where they can see that it will improve their working life. But that willingness cannot be taken for granted,” Rishworth said.

“Will they receive support and opportunities to build new skills? Will their knowledge and expertise still be valued? Will they share in the benefits being created? Without answers to these questions, workers will naturally lose trust in the process and become reluctant to engage with new technologies,” she said.
Greens leader David Shoebridge accused the government of “watching from the sidelines” while big companies slashed their workforce, demanding protection against surveillance and job cuts.
“When the government talks about asking employers nicely to consult staff, what it is really saying is that a worker who loses their job to an algorithm will have no legal recourse at all.
“We have seen Qantas, Canva, NAB and ANZ all firing Australian workers as part of offshoring and an AI rollout – it’s clear the time for optional guidelines has passed,” he said.
“Sharing the benefits of AI through better pay and shorter hours is a good idea, and it is exactly why it needs to be written into law instead of left to the goodwill of employers.”
The Reserve Bank this week reported it had seen “little evidence to date” of AI disrupting Australia’s labour market, but said the size and type of future impacts were “highly uncertain”.

The RBA – which last week warned the construction of datacentres and AI investment was fuelling inflation – said it saw “tentative signs” of impacts on certain roles, like clerks, computer programmers and call centre workers.

Qantas this week announced 850 job cuts which would target finance, human resources and marketing roles. Meanwhile, National Australian Bank announced 2,500 job losses and while Canva announced 1,200 layoffs.
All have been linked partly to the growth in AI.

Rishworth’s workplace guide says little about potential redundancies linked to AI, but warns employers they should be consulting with workers about the takeup of AI and what it might mean for their jobs. It especially raises concern about “entry-level work”, which the guide said may be “the first to be automated”.

articles.title: AMLC: No bank records of contractor, DPWH sending money to Romualdez
articles.summary: A witness from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) said Thursday the P560.5-million worth of remittances that went to the bank account of suspended Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez during…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 2:54pm

A witness from the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) said Thursday the P560.5-million worth of remittances that went to the bank account of suspended Leyte Representative Martin Romualdez during his tenure as House speaker from 2022 to 2025 were not related to flood control transactions.

AMLC financial investigator Atty. Jan Mark Busa made the testimony during the bail petition hearing of Romualdez, who is facing a P7.4-billion plunder charge alongside former Ako Bicol party-list Representative Zaldy Co, Romualdez's personal assistant Joselyn Tragua Sereño, and Felicito Cristobal Guevarra, president of Samchan Foreign Exchange Corporation, over their alleged links to the flood control kickback scheme.

During the cross-examination of Romualdez's counsel Atty. Rashel Ann Pomoy, Busa said the AMLC monitored P560 million worth of bank transactions recorded under the former House leader's bank accounts from September 2022 to March 2025.
Asked by Pomoy if it would be correct to say that the AMLC did not have findings that these P560-million remittances were related to flood control projects, Busa answered in the affirmative.
Busa, meanwhile, said AMLC was unable to trace money transfers to Romualdez by a contractor, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) or his co-accused Co.
Busa's investigation covered 1,951 financial transactions of Romualdez covering the period from 2022 to 2025.

Pomoy also asked Busa to confirm his statement in his judicial affidavit stating that the AMLC monitored P560 million worth of remittances that went through Romualdez's bank accounts from September 2022 to March 2025, or lower than the P7.4-billion plundered money that Ombudsman prosecutors are alleging.
Busa confirmed that he said, "There appears to be a huge disparity between the inflow and the amount charged of P7.4 billion."

Further, Busa denied that AMLC's record of Romualdez sending money to Golden Pheasant, the company which Ombudsman prosecutors allege was used by the Leyte congressman to purchase a property located at 30 Tamarind Road, South Forbes Park, Makati City that is partially funded by simulated dollar-to-peso transactions facilitated by Guevarra through Samchan. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: PNP on full alert in NCR, Regions 3, 4A starting Nov. 13 for ASEAN Summit 2026
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police (PNP) will place its units in Metro Manila, Central Luzon, and Calabarzon under full alert status starting Friday in preparation for the country's hosting of the 49th…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 2:45pm

The Philippine National Police (PNP) will place its units in Metro Manila, Central Luzon, and Calabarzon under full alert status starting Friday in preparation for the country's hosting of the 49th ASEAN Summit.
At a press briefing, PNP spokesperson Police Brigadier General Allen Rae Co said the full alert status will cover the following units:

items: National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO)
Police Regional Office 3
Police Regional Office 4A
all Camp Crame-based units.

blocks.text: The measure will remain in effect until November 19 but may be extended if necessary, according to the PNP.

According to Co, the full alert status would ensure that its units maintain their full personnel complement, particularly as police personnel from other regions have been deployed to augment security operations in Metro Manila.
“Ang ibig sabihin ng full alert status ay 100% present,” he said.
(Full alert status means 100% present.)
Meanwhile, the PNP sees low-level threats to the conduct of the ASEAN Summit-related activities.
“Meron po tayong low-level threats na tinitignan but nothing major. Normal threats na 'yung disorderly conduct, 'yung mga pwedeng people taking opportunity na para magnakaw,” he said.
(We have low-level threats that we are looking at but nothing major. Normal threats are disorderly conduct, people taking opportunity to steal.)
The PNP has deployed more than 19,000 personnel for the ASEAN Summit, with over 3,000 personnel from other government agencies providing augmentation.
This brings the total security deployment to nearly 23,000 personnel, covering crowd management, summit venues, billeting areas, hotels, and medical services. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to…

blocks.text: Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.

Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.

blocks.text: In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair

blocks.caption: US intelligence officials  had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang. Photograph: CTI/AFPTV/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.

US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.

Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.

The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …
Who is Alice Huang?

Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.

There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.

Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.
What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?

The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”

Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).

“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.

China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”
“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.
What approach has the US taken?

Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump. He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.

But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.

blocks.text: The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Researchers discover a potential diagnostic breakthrough for ovarian cancer, a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread. Photograph: Simon Dawson/PA

blocks.text: Researchers from the Hoag Family Cancer Institute have made a potential breakthrough in the early diagnosis of ovarian cancer – a disease often detected after it has spread.

For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.

Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.
The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.

blocks.text: What you need to know
Here is our rolling coverage from India on Thursday, November 12:

items: India's cabinet has passed plans to develop the 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' showcasing India's civilization journey
Two colonial-era blocks in Central Delhi, that earlier as government offices, are being transformed to house the museum
The first gallery under the project is expected to open next year

blocks.text: November 12, 2026
Mega museum on Indian civilization gets cabinet nod

blocks.caption: The first part of the large museum is expected to open up next yearImage: Sonu Mehta/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government has approved the development of a massive museum in the heart of India's capital, New Delhi, estimated to cost around $340 million (around €306 million).
The 'Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum' — which was first announced by Modi in 2023 — is being billed as the museum "with the largest display area in the world."

The Sanskrit name of the museum translates to 'India through the ages'. The project has been envisaged as the country's landmark museum, the government said, and will showcase elements of Indian history and civilization, which spans thousands of years.
Modi hails 'timeless richness' of Indian civilization
The century-old North and South Blocks in New Delhi's Raisina Hills — the seat of the Indian government — will be reused for the museum.

The colonial-era twin blocks once housed government offices, including Modi's own, before they were vacated over the last year as part of the Modi government's redesigning of India's hub of political power.
The Hindu nationalist government has long sought to emphasize India's pre-colonial cultural identity.

"Buildings that have been centres of governance will now become a place where millions can discover, experience and celebrate the timeless richness of our civilisation," Modi wrote on X on Wednesday night.

Calling the museum a "magnificent celebration" of India's "civilizational journey", Modi said the museum's galleries will bring to life aspects including ancient knowledge systems, mathematics, astronomy to architecture, art, languages and spirituality, through "immersive experiences."
Inaugural gallery to open in 2027
According to a press release from the Indian cabinet, the museum will encompass an area of nearly 178,509 square meters with the ability to welcome some 10 million visitors a year.

The finalization of the project isn't planned until 2030/31, but the first gallery on the theme of "adornment" will open its doors to the public next year, with more galleries gradually opening after that.

The content and collection analysis for the museum is currently underway, with the government having identified some 1.8 million objects for possible display from national and state museums, alongside archaeological and private collections.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Video of Nepal protest misrepresented as anti-Marcos rally
articles.summary: The original video posted on TikTok also shows that the crowd was not chanting Duterte’s name during the protest

blocks.text: Claim: A video shows a “chaotic” crowd at a rally held against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Manila.

Why we fact-checked this: The video bearing the claim has already received 399,000 views, 8,400 reactions, 1,900 shares, and 852 comments as of writing. It was posted on November 8 and continues to gain traction.

The crowd can be heard chanting “Duterte!” during the protest. Text on the Facebook reel reads, “Wala sa news! Philippines Manila updates today!!! Bulag pipi at bingi na si BBM matatapos ang taon walang makukulong kahit isa.”
(Not in the news! Philippines Manila updates today!!! [Bongbong Marcos] has become blind, mute, and deaf. The year is ending, and not a single person has been jailed.)
Additional text overlaid on the reel reads, “Grabe sobrang gulo. Ngayon lang to.”
(It’s incredibly chaotic. This has never happened before.)
Some Facebook users in the comments believed the video did show a protest against Marcos, with some questioning why the supposed protest was not reported on mainstream news agencies.

The facts: The video does not show an anti-Marcos rally in Manila in November 2026. It shows footage of a protest in Kathmandu, Nepal, in September 2025. The original video on TikTok also revealed that the crowd was not chanting the Duterte name while protesting.Fact-checking organizations have already discredited previous false posts misrepresenting videos of protests in Nepal as rallies in the Philippines. In November 2025, AFP Fact-check debunked a November 2025 post using the same video and falsely labeling it as an anti-corruption rally in the Philippines.
The user who posted the TikTok video told AFP that he was the one who filmed the footage of a “GenZ” protest against the government from his office on Madan Bhandari Road in Kathmandu, Nepal.

FactRakers also debunked the same post in November 2025, referencing Google Maps’ Street View images. Key landmarks, including the footbridge, traffic control booth, and the Parliament’s perimeter fence, show that the protest happened along Madan Bhandari Road in Kathmandu, Nepal, and not in Manila.

Protests: No major rallies directed against Marcos have been held as of November 2026. Instead, the current rallies focus on US President Donald Trump’s scheduled visit to the Philippines from November 16 to 18 for the 49th Leaders’ Summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and related meetings. (READ: [Rappler’s Best] Who’s coming to town?)
Activist group Gabriela staged a rally on November 9, and some groups are also set to hold a protest during the summit.
Previous fact checks: Rappler has fact-checked similar misrepresented videos of protests:

items: FACT CHECK: Nepal protest, Trillion Peso March misrepresented as recent rallies in PH
FACT CHECK: Videos of La Naval procession, Nepal protests misrepresented as rallies in PH
FACT CHECK: INC rally misrepresented as protest against VP Sara arrest warrant
FACT CHECK: Video of Peñafrancia procession misrepresented as rally in Metro Manila

blocks.text: – Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com
Angelee Kaye Abelinde is a student journalist based in Naga City, and an alumna of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.
