articles.title: Nvidia board reportedly deciding whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang as stock price plunges
articles.summary: The meeting comes after the executive and co-founder admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy

blocks.text: Nvidia’s board of directors met on Wednesday to decide whether to oust Jensen Huang as CEO of the world’s most valuable chip company, according to multiple reports, after a tumultuous week in which the executive and co-founder of the company admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The meeting marks ⁠a sharp shift from Sunday, when Nvidia’s board ​expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team, and the company’s stock slid more than 8% in after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal reported that ⁠the company was preparing to fire Huang.

If those losses hold, Nvidia will have lost about $600bn in market value since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang who is accused of being a Chinese spy.

“The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not ‌a tail risk,” said Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager and co-founder ‌of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares.
Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors. Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.

The company earlier this week appointed leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship. The firm directed Huang to continue to helm Nvidia as the investigation was ongoing.

blocks.caption: Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan in 2025. Photograph: TVBS/AP

blocks.text: Late on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

Huang is seen as the ambitious and visionary leader of Nvidia, a company he co-founded in 1993. His exit would leave a leadership vacuum at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex. He has no obvious successor, and personally owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company. Unlike many of his contemporaries at other major tech firms, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.

The entire artificial intelligence ecosphere relies on the company, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. It’s also one of the most valuable companies on earth, with a market cap of more than $4tn. Huang himself is one of the world’s richest people, with an estimated net worth of $148bn.

While Huang admitted to having an affair, he denies any knowledge that the woman allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is a businesswoman and head of Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed,.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last month. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: On Thursday a Taiwanese government minister said Alice Huang had visited Taiwan a total of eight times in 2024 and 2025, as he responded to questions about a New York Times report that claimed the US had advised Taiwan as early as 2024 to monitor her movements.

Chiu Chui-cheng, the Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) minister, said there were “no special flags” about her at the time, Chiu said, adding that “if we had any of the kind of critical intelligence … we would have definitely flagged her for heightened review.”

Jensen Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
Donald Trump has backed Huang, saying he had done “an incredible job” and is “an honorable guy”. Major tech industry players, including Elon Musk, have also thrown their support behind Huang.

Meanwhile, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren ⁠and Chris Coons have asked the Trump administration to preserve all documents tied to Nvidia’s chip ⁠exports to China, it was revealed late on Wednesday.

“This ‌incident raises significant ‌concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export ‌controls and protect our national security,” the senators said in the letter sent to commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, secretary of state Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
Nvidia did not immediately return request for comment.
With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

articles.title: Teenager in critical condition after likely ‘train surfing’ on Sydney Harbour Bridge, police say
articles.summary:
‘You just don’t mess or play with a 400-tonne train’, Sydney trains says as 17-year-old suffers multiple injuries to head, chest and pelvis

A 17-year-old boy is in a critical condition after…

blocks.text: A 17-year-old boy is in a critical condition after falling from the outside of a train on the Sydney Harbour Bridge while he was likely train surfing, NSW police say.

Around 11.30am on Thursday, emergency services were called to the railway corridor between Wynyard and Milsons Point train stations following reports someone had fallen from a northbound Tangara train onto the tracks on the bridge.

A multi-agency operation took place, with a Careflight helicopter landing at Bradfield Park a short time later with a medical team, including NSW ambulance paramedics who administered assistance on the bridge before carrying the teenager 400 metres to safety.

The boy was transported by road to Royal North Shore hospital where he was being treated for multiple injuries including to his head, chest and pelvis. He was in a critical condition on Thursday afternoon, the hospital confirmed.
Luke Barrett, a police transport command inspector, said the boy was hanging off the outside of the train when the incident occurred and it was “likely” he was train surfing at the time.
He was with two other people, Barrett said, who were assisting police with inquiries on Thursday afternoon. They had not been placed under arrest.

“Initial inquiries and review of CCTV [footage] and speaking to witnesses that were onboard the service indicates the male person was riding on the outside of the train in an activity which is commonly referred to as ‘buffer riding’,” Barrett said.

“We would really like to take this opportunity to encourage any person that is considering or actively engaged in this type of activity to not get caught up in the social media hype, in the videos that circulate around … glorifying this type of activity.

“This is highly dangerous, it carries an extreme level of risk and the consequences should something goes wrong, which [it is indicated] has happened here today, can result in very serious injuries or possible death.”
Barrett said train surfing, particularly on the rear carriages, had been increasing, particularly during school holidays and the warmer months.
Barrett said the boy had not become trapped under the train when he fell and it was a “relatively straightforward extrication”. He said inquiries would continue over the coming days.

In September, passengers were barred from using the rear carriages of Tangara or “T set” trains, which run on the eastern suburbs, Illawarra, north shore, western and northern lines, including between Wynyard and Milsons Point, to prevent people from riding on the back of them.
The policy was in force in a limited way for select weekend and night-time services, but was extended to every Tangara train for the school holiday period.
Train-surfing on Tangara trains has been popularised on social media where people have posted their experiences illegally “buffer riding”.
In November last year, the New South Wales government announced new safety devices would be installed across the fleet to physically prevent people from accessing the back of trains.

The specially designed “nose cone” attachments block access to the tread plate between carriages - the area often used by “buffer riders” or “train surfers”, who cling to the outside of moving trains in order to film social-media videos.
after newsletter promotion
There have been 12 serious injuries in New South Wales in the past five years, including a 13-year-old boy who fell from a train at Caringbah last September.
The acting chief executive of Sydney Trains, Jas Tumbler, said it was a “really tragic incident” that had occurred and said his thoughts were with the boy, his family and friends.
He said it had also been a “difficult situation” for first responders, who had to move the boy several hundred metres to safety.
“You just don’t mess or play with a 400-tonne train; there will always be significant consequences and these are life changing events that occur,” he said.
Tumbler said there had been around 600 incidents of train surfing in 2025 and were close to 150 this year, which was a large reduction.
But he added “each one of these incidents comes with a significant amount of risk”.
“It’s just not worth the five seconds of social media fame that you’re looking for,” he said.
“We’re doing everything we can to prevent this activity … but it’s a challenge, and we’re always chasing our tail in this space.”
Tumbler said transport for NSW were still working to install CCTV footage across all Tangara trains, which it hoped would be completed by the end of next year.

articles.title: Army soldier faces sanctions over dog-killing video: What we know so far
articles.summary: Following a viral dog-killing video in Zamboanga del Sur, advocates push for animal cruelty charges and a lifetime pet-ownership ban against a Philippine Army soldier
articles.byline: Arabella Grace Sta Ana, Neo Croox

blocks.text: Following a viral dog-killing video in Zamboanga del Sur, advocates push for animal cruelty charges and a lifetime pet-ownership ban against a Philippine Army soldier

items: A Philippine Army soldier has been relieved from duty and is under investigation for allegedly killing a dog, with potential criminal charges for animal cruelty.
Animal welfare groups are pushing for accountability, with calls for criminal charges and a lifetime ban on the soldier from keeping animals.
The Army emphasizes its commitment to addressing misconduct and is strengthening its social media policy to prevent similar incidents.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – A Philippine Army soldier accused of killing a dog in a viral social media video has been relieved from his duties and is facing an administrative investigation, with possible criminal charges over the alleged animal cruelty.

Army spokesperson Colonel Louie Dema-ala said on Tuesday, November 10, that the soldier, assigned to the 1st Infantry Division in Zamboanga del Sur, had been relieved from his duties pending the resolution of his administrative case.
According to a news report, the soldier is staying at the division headquarters at Camp Major Cesar Sang-an in Zamboanga del Sur while the case is being investigated.
“The minimum would be demotion from his rank,” Dema-ala said during a press briefing at Camp Aguinaldo in Quezon City, adding that complainants may also pursue a separate criminal case against him.
“The Philippine Army strongly condemns any act of animal cruelty,” he added.
Dema-ala also said personnel found responsible would face appropriate administrative and disciplinary sanctions, as well as applicable legal consequences under existing laws and regulations.

Animal welfare group Strategic Power for Animal Respondents (SPAR) Philippines identified the soldier as Private First Class Ruiz in an October 26 Facebook post calling for accountability over the incident.
The group said it received information about the soldier from individuals who claimed to know him after the incident was initially reported to Bataan Animal Welfare.
The Army initially sought to verify the identities of those involved, including the individual who recorded the footage.

Another report interviewed a relative of the soldier, identified only by the alias Camille, who expressed shock over the video. She said their family also had pet dogs and believed the soldier should be held accountable.
SPAR also called on the Armed Forces of the Philippines to impose disciplinary action on the soldier.
The group said military personnel are expected to know and follow the law, and stressed that animal cruelty should never be treated as entertainment or as content for social media attention.
It called for an investigation and for the soldier to be held accountable if the allegations are proven.
The Animal Kingdom Foundation (AKF) said it intends to file a criminal complaint against those involved in the incident.

AKF lawyer Heidi Marquez-Caguioa said animal cruelty cases are often difficult to pursue because witnesses are reluctant to come forward or identify themselves. The group also emphasized that military personnel are covered by animal welfare laws like everyone else.
People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) Asia said an administrative penalty would not be enough.

“Dogs depend on humans for protection, and this dog suffered a terrifying and painful death at the hands of someone sworn to serve and protect. Demotion alone cannot deliver justice for a dog whose life was violently taken,” PETA Asia president Jason Baker said in a statement.

The group is calling for animal cruelty charges and a lifetime ban preventing the soldier from keeping animals. It also urged the public to report any witnessed cruelty to animals to the nearest police station and to PETA at 0999-888-7382.

Under the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by Republic Act No. 10631, a person convicted of subjecting an animal to cruelty, maltreatment, or neglect faces one year, six months, and one day to two years in prison, a fine of up to P100,000, or both if the animal dies.
Heavier penalties of two years and one day to three years in prison, a fine of up to P250,000, or both apply when the offense is committed by a government personnel, among others.

The soldier remains at the 1st Infantry Division headquarters at Camp Major Cesar Sang-an in Zamboanga del Sur while he awaits the final disposition of his administrative case, as well as possible criminal proceedings that complainants may initiate.
The Army said it would not tolerate misconduct within its ranks and that personnel found guilty would be held accountable, with due process observed.
Dema-ala also said the Army is strengthening its social media policy to remind personnel of their responsibilities and prevent similar incidents.
The Army has recorded more than 300 violations of the policy, all under investigation, with 24 personnel already sanctioned for various violations. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Ukraine's power supply close to critical as Russian strikes bring darkness and cold
articles.summary: For parents in parts of Ukraine, trying to lead a normal family life with just a few hours of power each day is taking its toll.

blocks.text: Daryna Kulchytska is a mum under pressure. A single parent in a seventh floor flat in Kyiv trying to feed two lively kids and ensure they do their homework. But Daryna also faces the added strain of a deadline she can't even be certain of.

All she knows is soon the lights will go out, the sockets will lose power, the wi-fi will drop, and the taps will run dry. Tonight, the electricity has kept flowing an hour longer than advertised, but Daryna's still racing to serve dinner and finish her own work from home.
"The last few days it was only four or five hours we had power, but it's not at the same times. For two hours we have electricity, then for eight hours we don't."
This rolling schedule of planned power cuts has been in place since October, as Russia intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy grid. Ukraine has responded by striking Russian oil refineries.

Officials are concerned that life will quickly become unsustainable for millions of Ukrainians if power supplies cannot be maintained for at least four hours per day. Some privately warn that's close already, as some families are living with outages of up to 20 hours in Kyiv.

The power cuts were introduced earlier this year than last winter, and they're already lasting longer - making homes like Daryna's darker and colder. She's wrapped in layers of clothing and a heavy coat - the temperature is dropping, indoors and out.
Just before 7:30pm, there's a click and that's it - darkness until dawn.

The lift doesn't work, the water will stop flowing because electricity is needed to pump it to their flat. So the torches and LED candles come out and Daryna, her son Kyryll and daughter Olena gather for a card game of Uno before an early night.
Twelve-year-old Kyryll, speaking perfect English learned during two years living in the US, is frank about the disruption.

"There's no light, no water, no heat, no electricity. And no fun. All the fun got sucked out with the electricity," he says. "We have a lot of board games. We have a whole shelf, but we've played them like a hundred thousand times already."
Many families sit in the shadows as blackouts sweep entire neighbourhoods, smothering homes and streets in darkness.
"You look outside and sometimes you see nothing. You have a big city around but you see nothing because there's no light," Daryna says.
Kyiv has been worst hit - its metro trains and trolleybuses at times brought to a standstill. Nationwide, hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians have gone without power in recent weeks.

We saw why on a visit to one of Ukraine's largest power stations, barely standing after a recent ballistic missile strike - the most powerful and devastating attack of Russia's campaign against Ukrainian energy targets.

The enormous plant - which we've been asked not to name for security reasons - has been reduced to a pile of twisted metal and broken pipes, its turbines buried in rubble, taking the site completely off line.
Volodymyr Kovalenko was on duty in the control room keeping the plant working when the missiles hit at 3am.
"It was a very powerful attack. We'd never experienced anything like it. We'd had strikes before – part of the roof had collapsed, it was pretty grim. But this time it was particularly severe."
Kovalenko, who followed in his parents' footsteps and has worked at the site for 25 years, says the damage is heartbreaking, though he's confident it can be repaired.

But the work is being hampered by air raids every 15-30 minutes – seven times during our four-hour visit. Each warning of drones and further missiles forces teams to down tools and dive for cover, though during our visit all were shot down or flew on towards other targets.
If there isn't time to reach the site's main shelter, the workers hide in the foundations of its towering chimneys.

"It's very difficult," says Vadym Bobyr, who is leading the recovery effort. "You've mentally prepared yourself to do a particular job, and then… the air raid siren goes off, and you have to get out as quickly as possible."
The 39-year-old, who has worked here half his life, is dwarfed by the mangled ruins and daunted by the challenge of rebuilding the plant.
"It's emotionally difficult, because we've already repaired all this, got it running again, and now it's happened all over again. It hurts, but we keep working and getting things done."
As we speak there's another alert - an incoming Banderol cruise missile.

The workers dart through the maze of passages and pipework but there isn't time to reach a shelter - one of the plant's thickest walls will have to do for cover. The missile was eventually intercepted 5km (3 miles) away.
Energy workers are at enormous risk. Since August there have been almost daily attacks on power facilities, claiming several lives every week. And it's getting more dangerous.

On the edge of the site, with the latest threat over, a team returns to reinstating the power lines feeding the national grid. But they won't be carrying electricity from the shattered plant before the end of this winter, at least.

President Volodymyr Zelensky says Ukraine still has enough generating capacity to meet electricity demand - the problem is getting it to homes and businesses when so many power lines and substations have been hit. Russia is using "waiter drones" that cling to pylons and cables and go undetected until Russia decides to detonate them.

Maxim Timchenko, CEO of DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said Russia was already putting the degraded electricity grid under even greater pressure than last year, and that overstretched air defences were unable to protect all of Ukraine's critical infrastructure.
"What is different is the scale of attacks and the different types of weapons used in these attacks. This is what is the difference - they've doubled in power and in scale".
He said rebuilding the damaged power station would take at least until next summer, because workers under sustained attack were limited to only one or two productive hours per day.
"We are fighting for survival of not only the whole country but ordinary people, especially during winter," Timchenko says.

Kovalenko echoes the sense of mission about trying to keep the lights on. "Energy is the foundation of everything - people's lives, the state. Nothing can function without it. I've dedicated my entire life to this".
Many are choosing to leave the capital, or Ukraine altogether, to avoid months of bitter cold. Daryna, Kyryll and Olena know the winter has barely begun.
"It's the worst feeling" Kyryll says. "When I get home from school, I'm tired. I lay in my bed. Bam! Air alarm. Bam! No lights. Bam! A lot of homework. Bam!"

When the children are in bed Daryna confides her thoughts of moving to somewhere safer, or warmer. She's torn by the desire to stay at home - close to friends and relatives - and the worry of how unbearable life may become.
The strain is damaging her mental health, she tells me, and she fears the impact on Kyryll and Olena, who suffers nightmares. Still, Daryna remains defiant despite the darkness.

"I don't want to live without light. But actually people in Ukraine say, OK, without light, but without Russians. Yes, we're scared, we're scared a lot. But better for us to be without power, but [also] without Russians."
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko, Kamila Hrabchuk and Daniel Wittenberg

articles.title: Where the US's war with Iran stands after the midterms
articles.summary: Almost nine months after it began, the war in Iran has calmed to the point where Donald Trump sees an end. But with the key issues of the conflict unresolved and political change in the US, what is…

image.caption: Donald Trump endured a difficult midterm loss, with Iran a key issueImage: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US-Israel war with Iran, according to US President Donald Trump, "is effectively over" in a military sense. Trump's secretary of state, Marco Rubio, backed up the president, saying there is "no need for major combat operations" in Iran because economic pressure and negotiations between the warring parties are proving effective.

However, Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, has denied negotiations are even taking place. "All American claims about the continuation of negotiations with Iran are aimed at easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices," he told Lebanese channel Al Mayadeen.
Is the Iran war actually over?

While neither side has claimed the conflict is concluded in every sense, Ian Kelly, a former US ambassador who now works at Northwestern University in the US, considers the current situation is something like a "virtual ceasefire." He added that there is currently a significant deescalation but that the central issues are unresolved.

"I wouldn't say the war is over. I would say there's no shooting going on, nothing really significant," Kelly told DW. "But the real issue is opening up the Strait of Hormuz. What Iran wants, of course, is for the United States to withdraw its massive strike forces from the Gulf. But that won't happen until Iran agrees to open the Strait of Hormuz."

A critical shipping lane between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the Strait of Hormuz has been a focal point in the US-Iran conflict. Iran's attacks on commercial ships in the strait have led to higher oil prices and have had other economic impacts that have affected living costs in the US and around the world.

Kelly, who also held several high-level roles at the US State Department, thinks the US midterm election results, which will see the Democrats take control of the House and Senate next year after catastrophic losses for Trump's Republicans, means Iran is sitting tight.

"I think that Iran is in a wait-and-see moment to see if the war will wind down because Congress acts to either cut off the funding or severely limit the funding," he said. But with Iran's resources also dwindling, it's a game of cat and mouse.
What has this conflict meant for Donald Trump and what's next for the US?
Trump and his party need the war to end, according to Kelly, for political reasons, as well as strategic.
"As long as the war is not resolved, it's going to be a real sticking point for the Republicans as they look at [the election in] 2028. They have to wrap it up before then," he said.

"A major contributing factor to the Republican defeat was how Trump has not followed through on some of his promises made in 2024. One of the big ones was no more forever wars, and he just went off and started another war that doesn't seem to have an exit strategy. It has weakened the Republican Party."
Trump weakened: Is Europe safer now?
The imminent change in US politics will naturally have military consequences long before the 2028 election.

”There is little likelihood that Congress will continue to fund this war at the kind of levels that they have been," said Kelly. "That's another reason that Iran is sitting back and just waiting to see where this all comes out."
What needs to happen for a compromise to be reached?

While the US administration claims it is happy with a status quo of containment through land and sea blockades, Kelly believes the authority of Trump and his party will be further diminished if the US can't achieve concrete progress on its stated main goals: gaining full control of the Strait of Hormuz and forcing Iran to give up its enriched uranium.
"Both of those are quite possible," Kelly said, adding that even attempting to achieve them threatens the current relative calm.

"The White House has really painted itself in a corner here by stressing that the main goal is to deny Iran a nuclear weapon. I don't see that as something that Iran is going to negotiate away, which means that they [the US] will probably have to use military force again. The White House is in a real pickle."
But there is also the question of how long Iran can bear the economic burden of the war without reaching a deal.

"Iran's limitation in the Strait of Hormuz is economic rather than military, because continuing the war has a significant impact on its economy," Ali Mohammadi, an expert in Iranian affairs based in France, told DW earlier this week.
Nevertheless, the strait remains a key source of leverage for Iran in any future negotiations.
What would the end of the Iran War mean for the world economy?
Kelly doesn't see the economic strain of the war subsiding anytime soon, especially in oil markets.

blocks.caption: The Strait of Hormuz remains key to bothe Iran and the USImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: "The real issue for the markets is that as long as it remains a phony war, it's very difficult to see oil prices lowering. The prices that are being charged now factor in the possible return to instability, so it has to be some kind of agreement where all sides and the oil markets are confident that we see a return to status quo. It's going to be difficult to restore the markets' confidence that these tankers won't be shot at again," Kelly said.

Given the global consequences of the conflict, Kelly expects it to be a hot topic at this month's APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) summit in Shenzhen, where Trump and his counterparts in Russia and China, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, will reportedly meet.

"I think Russia is interested in keeping the United States tied down like this. China, though, is interested in resolving it because they are a big customer," he said. A G20 summit in Miami follows the APEC meeting in December.

While the impasse between Iran and the US shows little sign of being broken, the fighting has calmed, for now at least. What happens in the coming weeks in the meeting rooms of Shenzhen and Miami currently looks more critical to finding a solution than what happens on Iranian territory or waterways.

articles.title: Chiz cautions senator-judges against harsh questioning of witnesses
articles.summary: "An answer which may be unsatisfactory is not inherently contemptible."

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 1:35pm
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian (left) and Senate Impeachment Presiding Officer Francis Escudero (right) at the Senate impeachment court on Nov. 12, 2026.
Senate PRIB
MANILA, Philippines — After tense exchanges at the Senate impeachment court, presiding officer Chiz Escudero reminded senator-judges and lawyers to exercise restraint in questioning witnesses.
Escudero said witnesses in Vice President Sara Duterte's trial are entitled to protection from insulting questions and harsh treatment, even when their answers are unsatisfactory.
"The chair wishes to emphasize that an answer which may be unsatisfactory is not inherently contemptible," Escudero said.
He cited Section 3, Rule 132 of the Rules on Evidence, which outlines the rights and obligations of witnesses during judicial proceedings.
"A witness must answer questions, although his answer may tend to establish a claim against him," Escudero said, quoting the provision.
The rule also protects witnesses from irrelevant, improper or insulting questions, as well as harsh or insulting behavior during examination.
It further limits questioning to matters pertinent to the case and provides protections against self-incrimination and questions that could unfairly damage a witness's reputation.
Chiz acknowledges own impatience

Escudero acknowledged that he, too, had shown frustration during earlier proceedings, when defense witnesses struggled to answer questions about properties linked to Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

"The chair wishes to remind the members of this court as well, including the presiding officer himself, who stated that his patience was wearing thin the other day, that we are sitting as senator-judges in a trial," he said.

During Tuesday's hearing, Escudero told Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan that his patience was running out after she repeatedly struggled to recall details of her former partnership in an accounting firm that audited companies linked to Duterte.
Other senator-judges also questioned Bajan's recollection, particularly her difficulty confirming documents and transactions involving the firm.

The previous day, Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin faced similar scrutiny over his inconsistent testimony about properties declared in Duterte's SALN and his inability to recall details of his overseas travels.

The witnesses were presented by the defense under Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which covers allegations of ill-gotten wealth and failure to fully disclose Duterte's assets and liabilities.

Escudero's reminder came as the impeachment court continued hearing testimony on those allegations, underscoring the obligation of senator-judges to ensure fair treatment of witnesses while examining the evidence before them.

articles.title: New York building collapse kills at least two, officials say
articles.summary: A dangerous search for survivors continues after a three-storey building collapsed in Brooklyn on Wednesday afternoon.

blocks.text: At least two people have died and more than 17 others are injured after a building in New York City collapsed into an open construction site, officials have said.

It sparked a massive search-and-rescue operation, with more than 250 first responders at the scene in Brooklyn, trying to find survivors who may have been trapped under the rubble of the three-storey building.
Hours later, aerial video showed firefighters pulling a survivor, covered in dust, out of the debris on a stretcher.
Authorities are yet to determine what caused the sudden collapse at about 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT) on Wednesday.
The rescue mission has been described as "extremely dangerous" by New York City Fire Department (FDNY) Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore.
She added that people from the collapsed building and also the construction site had been trapped.
"Members have been working methodically and haven't stopped since they arrived this afternoon," Bonsignore said.

Some pictures of the collapsed building, on Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn, show an entire side of it gone, with bedrooms and closets exposed. Among the debris, smashed concrete and twisted metal, are household items and clothes.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani joined emergency responders at the scene, praising them for their rapid response.
They "arrived in under a minute and have spent hours working in dangerous and highly technical conditions to rescue New Yorkers," he later wrote on X.
The Brooklyn building was built in 1930, city records show, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 1:11pm
A 50-year-old male passenger bound for Hong Kong was arrested after allegedly making a bomb joke at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) Terminal 1, airport police said Thursday.

In a statement, the Philippine National Police Aviation Security Group (AVSEGROUP) said the incident occurred at the airport's departure area Tuesday while an airline passenger service agent was explaining restrictions on dangerous goods and electronic devices.
The passenger allegedly told the airline personnel, "Bomba, may bomba 'yan (It has a bomb)."
AVSEGROUP personnel investigated the matter and coordinated with the Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team.
After the inspection of the passenger's baggage and the surrounding area, authorities declared these clear of explosives and incendiary materials.
The passenger was arrested and brought to the NAIA Police Station 1 for disposition.
A criminal complaint is being prepared against him for alleged violation of the Anti-Bomb Joke Law in relation to Article 287 of the Revised Penal Code or Unjust Vexation.
AVSEGROUP director Police Brigadier Dionisio Bartolome Jr. stressed that bomb jokes are never taken lightly as these can cause unnecessary alarm and disrupt airport operations. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV returns to Peru to a big welcome, calls it his 'homeland'
articles.summary: An estimated 3 million people greeted Pope Leo XIV in Lima as the Peruvian-citizen pontiff began a six-day homecoming visit to the country where he spent two decades as a missionary and bishop.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV holds Peruvian citizenship and called the country home for over two decadesImage: Simone Risoluti/Vatican Media/AFP

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV opened the Peruvian leg of his South America tour on Wednesday, telling crowds in Lima that returning to the country where he served for two decades felt like coming home.
The Vatican estimated that about 3 million people lined his motorcade route, the Associated Press reported.
What did he say?
Leo holds Peruvian citizenship and spent more than two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and later as bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo before becoming pope.
Also a US citizen, he is the first pope from either the United States or Peru.
He sang Peru's national anthem with President Keiko Fujimori at the presidential palace.
"Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you," he said, adding that he was "also returning to my homeland."
Leo urged Peruvians to "cultivate honesty, integrity," and to accept that "no one has all the answers."

blocks.caption: As bishop, Leo XIV, then Robert Prevost, had repeatedly criticized Fujimori’s late father, former President Alberto FujimoriImage: Luis Acosta/AFP

blocks.text: He also called for stronger disaster prevention in a country regularly hit by El Nino-linked floods and landslides.
Fujimori said Peru must face the “unfinished task” of reconciliation after decades of insurgent violence, state abuses and sharp political divisions.
What is happening in Peru?
The welcome comes as many Peruvians are weary of their leaders.
The country has had nine presidents since July 2016, and homicide rates have nearly doubled in five years.
Political science professor Alonso Cardenas told AP he sees "no sign of a reaction, no strategy" from Fujimori's government.

blocks.caption: Peru remains a majority Catholic country, making up about 67% of the populationImage: Anthony Nino De Guzman/AFP

blocks.text: Notably, the Catholic Church is more credible than any other Peruvian institution, theology professor Veronique Lecaros told AP, even as Pew data show Catholics falling from 76% of the population to about 67%.

Leo's six-day stay includes a trip to 3,700 meters (about 12,140 feet), considered risky after Leo had part of a lung removed in mid-October because of a malignant tumor. He is due back at the Vatican on November 17.
Pope Leo starts jam-packed South America tour just weeks after surgery

articles.title: Greta Thunberg joins opposition to Pax Silica ahead of Philippines' signing
articles.summary: The Philippines is expected to sign the Pax Silica framework before the end of 2026, though not during the ASEAN Summit.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:35pm
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg speaks to the media as she arrives at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, on Nov. 10, 2026.
AFP / Ozan Kose

MANILA, Philippines — Renowned Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg has joined calls to reject Pax Silica, a US-led initiative to secure global semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains.
"Labor, land, and minerals should serve the people and the planet, not fuel the wars and ambitions of imperialist powers," Thunberg said in a social media video posted Wednesday, November 11.
As the Philippines moves toward joining the agreement later this year, Thunberg appeared alongside climate activists and organizers Mitzi Jonelle Tan, Mikaela Loach, Adrian Bonifacio and Kim Saira.
The activists also expressed support for protests against US President Donald Trump's upcoming visit to the Philippines.
Trump is expected to arrive in Manila for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit, with protests planned for Tuesday, November 17.
Although the Philippines is not expected to sign the Pax Silica framework agreement during the summit, the country's Board of Investments expects the signing to take place before the end of 2026.

Drawing opposition. Under the proposed framework, the Philippines has put forward plans for a 4,000-acre industrial center within the Luzon Economic Corridor to support advanced electronics manufacturing.

The project would begin with a 1,620-hectare hub in New Clark City, Tarlac, where development has faced controversy over alleged possible environmental degradation and the displacement of farming and fishing communities.
The Philippines' hub would be the first site developed among members of the Pax Silica consortium.

articles.summary: The Department of Energy (DOE) has revived its coal auction, including coal blocks in Semirara Island in Antique, despite concerns about the rule that requires mining companies to surrender their…

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 12:25pm

The Department of Energy (DOE) has revived its coal auction, including coal blocks in Semirara Island in Antique, despite concerns about the rule that requires mining companies to surrender their assets to the government.
In a notice of bidding issued on Nov. 10, the auction is pursuant to DOE and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources Joint Administrative Order No. 2026-01.

The bidding covers 10 coal blocks in Semirara Island in Caluya, Antique; three coal blocks in Amulung and Iguig in Cagayan; and five blocks in Benito Soliven, Naguilian, and Cauayan in Isabela Province.
According to DOE's timeline, the pre-bid conference will be held on November 13 and the deadline for submission of bids is December 11.
The bid opening date will also be on December 11.
The declaration of the highest-rated qualified bidder will be on December 28.
Meanwhile, the notice of award is scheduled on January 11, 2027.

“The DOE reserves the right to accept or reject any bid and to modify or amend this NOB, instruction to bidders or any related documents, and to suspend or annul the bid round at any time prior to the award, without incurring any liability to the affected bidders or any obligation to inform the bidder/s,” the notice read.

Consunji-led Semirara Mining and Power Corporation (SMPC) earlier cried foul over the latest bidding rules requiring the company to surrender its assets to the government if it joins the auction for Semirara Island’s mines.
SMPC also said the shift to the highest bidder from the most capable mining outfit as the main award criterion early this year “is puzzling."

The Japanese Chamber of Commerce and Industry of the Philippines, Inc. also raised questions over the rule requiring the surrender of assets, noting that this could affect the financial position of existing operators. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Alleged hacks hit at most 20 government agencies – CICC
articles.summary: Only 10 government agencies have so far filed personal data breach notifications with the National Privacy Commission.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:20pm
CICC says investigators are checking whether some purportedly stolen data are old leaks being recycled.
LagartoFilm / GettyImages via Canva

MANILA, Philippines — Hackers have claimed breaches of around 20 government agencies, about twice the number that have formally reported data incidents to the privacy regulator, the head of the government’s cybercrime coordinating body said.
Investigators are also checking whether some of the supposedly stolen data are "old exploits" passed off as new.

Renato Paraiso, executive director of the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC), said in a radio interview that the 20 agencies hit by breaches are based on alleged hacks whose authors posted purported data as proof.

"Based on the various alleged hacks and incidents — along with the alleged information they claim to have obtained, which is being presented as evidence — there are quite a number of them; around 20," Paraiso said in Filipino on dzBB Super Radyo.

The official tally of 10, meanwhile, came from government agencies that believed citizens' personal information had been compromised, which legally requires them to notify the National Privacy Commission (NPC).

The NPC said on Tuesday, November 10, it had received breach notifications from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the DICT, the Presidential Commission on Good Government, the Department of Labor and Employment, PAGCOR, the Department of Justice, the Philippine Coast Guard, the Department of Trade and Industry and Phivolcs.

The vulnerabilities exposed by the breaches in the BIR and SEC have "not just been contained but also remediated," Paraiso said, adding that investigators are still trying to identify the real identities of those responsible for the hacks.

Paraiso confirmed that some data had appeared to be stolen but said investigators were looking at several aspects: whether the datasets were new or “just being recycled to make it look like they hacked our government."
They are also reviewing whether the breaches involve personal information, as in the BIR and SEC cases, he added.
The CICC head said they stepped in because the incidents had risen to the level of cybercrime, and was working with other agencies to identify the people behind the groups.

The Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) said that it is already looking into possible exposure of taxpayer profile information after recent incidents of cybersecurity attack early this month.

"The initial findings further indicate that certain taxpayer profile information may have been exposed. The BIR, in coordination with the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) and the Department of Information and Technology - National Computer Emergency Response Team (DICT-NCERT), is conducting a forensic investigation to verify the source and extent of any unauthorized access," the BIR said in a statement.

articles.title: Defense witness says he 'partly paid' VP Sara's husband for P200K Ginza meal
articles.summary: A defense witness on Thursday said he "partly" reimbursed Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, for the P200,000 credit card bill for a meal in Ginza, Tokyo in Japan.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 12:12pm
A defense witness on Thursday said he "partly" reimbursed Atty. Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, for the P200,000 credit card bill for a meal in Ginza, Tokyo in Japan.
Atty. Anel Antero, a suppossed close friend of the Vice President and her husband, made the testimony during Day 43 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Antero testified that he was with Carpio and their nine other law school friends when they dined in Ginza and used Carpio’s credit card to pay for the bill. He said he later reimbursed Carpio with 40,000 Japanese Yen or around P16,000.
“Naalala ko po ang naging share ko po ay apat na lapad. That’s 40,000 Yen,” Antero said during direct examination of Lindon Bacquel.
“Sa pagkakaalam ko po, lahat naman po kami na contribute,” Antero added.
Private prosecutor Virgil Ligutan, in cross examination, asked Antero if he could provide a photo of him showing that he was with the 11 people who dined in Ginza with Carpio.
To which Antero replied, “wala po akong dalang photograph.”
(I don’t have any photograph with me.)
During the questioning of Ligutan, Antero also said that he received compensation from Carpio since Antero works in Carpio’s law firm.
But when Ligutan asked Antero if he received over P580,000 remittance from Carpio based on Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC), Antero did not give a categorical answer.
“Honestly, I don't recall,” Antero said.
Ligutan said such money transfer happened in July 2020 based on AMLC records.
Antero responded by saying “I still don’t recall.”

Defense counsel Bacquel objected in many instances by questioning the relevance of Ligutan’s questions, but Ligutan cited the Constitutional provision mandating public officials and their family members to lead a modest life and refrain from ostentatious display of wealth.

“This is central to the unexplained wealth, your honor. This is in the law: public officials and members of their family should lead a modest life. How is that irrelevant? Being the spouse of the the Vice President does not make him immune from the requirements of leading a modest life, your honor,” Ligutan said.
Bacquel, however, argued that Antero’s testimony is limited to the Ginza meal, not the Constitutional provisions. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos asks patience over ASEAN Summit 'disruptions'
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday appealed for the public's patience amid disruptions caused by the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 11:33am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday appealed for the public's patience amid disruptions caused by the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit.
In his blog, Marcos said the disruptions are only temporary and that the policies to be crafted during the Summit would bring corresponding benefits.
"Bagama’t may kaunting maaabala nitong susunod na araw, pansamantala lamang ito, kaunting pasensya lang," Marcos said.
(Although there will be some disruptions over the next few days, it will only be temporary, just a little patience.)
"Tiyak ko na mas matimbang pa rin ang mga benepisyong matatamasa natin mula sa mga polisiyang mapagkakasunduan at sa mga trabahong malilikha," he added.
(I am sure that the benefits we will enjoy from the policies that will be agreed upon and the jobs that will be created will outweigh them.)

Marcos pointed out that the Summit has generated jobs and income to Filipinos, particularly the micro, small, and medium enterprises; those in the fashion, food, transport, and hospitality industries; and artists and craftsmen.
He added that the Summit will also give opportunity for the country to boost its tourism industry.

Vendors in Pasay City and Parañaque City are not allowed to sell during the summit. The Department of Social Work and Development — National Capital Region (DSWD-NCR) has distributed family food packs and financial assistance to about 30 vendors in Pasay as compensation for expected lost income during the summit.
The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority also issued road closures, truck routes, stop-and-go scheme for the ASEAN Summit.
Amid backlash, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro had said the government is conducting clearing operations to ensure the security of world leaders who will attend the Summit.
Marcos announced that preparations for the ASEAN Summit is now complete.
"Ito ang pagkakataon para sa mga bansa sa ating rehiyon na mag-usap, magkaunawaan, at magtulungan upang humanap ng mga solusyon sa mga problemang pare-pareho nating kinakaharap," Marcos said.
(This is an opportunity for countries in our region to talk, understand, and work together to find solutions to the problems we all face.)

"Bilang host ng 49th ASEAN Summit, mayroon din tayong napakalaking pagkakataon na manguna sa paghubog ng agenda at bigyang prayoridad ang mga usaping pinakamahalaga sa ating mga kababayan tulad ng presyo ng langis at pagkain, seguridad, agrikultura, trabaho at kabuhayan," he added.

(As the host of the 49th ASEAN Summit, we also have a great opportunity to take the lead in shaping the agenda and give priority to the issues most important to our countrymen such as oil and food prices, security, agriculture, employment and livelihoods.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital kills at least six, Gaza civil defence agency says
articles.summary: The strike hit the surgery department of the hospital in Khan Younis, wounding at least 20 people and causing extensive damage, a spokesperson says.

blocks.text: At least six people have been killed after an Israeli airstrike hit a building at Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza, an official from the Hamas-run civil defence agency has said.
The strike hit the surgery department of the hospital in Khan Younis, wounding at least 20 people and causing extensive damage, spokesperson Mahmoud Basal told news agency AFP.
A surgeon is reported to be among those who were killed during the strike early on Thursday.
There has been no immediate response from the Israeli military. The BBC has contacted the Israel Defense Forces for comment.
The BBC is prevented by Israel from reporting independently from inside the Gaza Strip, and is unable to verify details of the incident.

Recovery work is carried out by the Civil Defence in Gaza, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry. Its efforts have been supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Nasser Hospital, the largest in southern Gaza, was hit by a double Israeli strike in August 2025, which killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers.

Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite a ceasefire agreement in October last year. More than 1,600 people have been killed since then, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
The humanitarian crisis in Gaza has also worsened from recent heavy rains that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents that were housing displaced families.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,645 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday decided not to present a witness from Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) for her impeachment trial.

Paul Roderick Ysmael, senior vice president of the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), won’t stand as a defense witness anymore because it was already established that Poa wrote a letter to the BPI about the bank accounts of the Vice President and her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte.

“The reason being that the only purpose for this witness was to authenticate my letter, Your Honor, and I believe the records would bear that during interpellation, I was already asked about the letter, and I have admitted in open court that I wrote that letter,” Poa told the Senate impeachment court.

articles.title: Witnesses' unsatisfactory answers not contemptible -- Escudero
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said Thursday that answers of witnesses that are deemed unsatisfactory by senator-judges do not constitute grounds for contempt.

blocks.text: Published November 12, 2026 11:16am
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said Thursday that answers of witnesses that are deemed unsatisfactory by senator-judges do not constitute grounds for contempt.

Escudero said this on the 43rd day of the impeachment trial, stressing that all witnesses are entitled to the rights listed under Rule 132, Section 3, of the Rules on Evidence, which have suppletory application to the proceedings, even as they took an oath before the court to testify truthfully and to answer all questions.

“The Chair wishes to emphasize that an answer which may be unsatisfactory is not inherently contemptible. Supreme Court cases have cautioned courts to use the power of contempt with the highest restraint,” the presiding officer said.
Escudero likewise reminded the members of the court, including himself, who earlier said that his patience was “wearing thin,” that they are sitting as senator-judges in a trial.
“Our rules behoove us to receive and evaluate the evidence with impartiality and, due to the often lengthy examination by both parties, with utmost patience as well,” he added.

On Tuesday, senator-judges called out Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan, a witness fielded by the defense, for supposedly being evasive and taking a long time to respond to questions being asked during the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Escudero back then said that his patience was “wearing thin,” considering the repeated answers of the witness that she could not remember details or is not familiar with documents presented by private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia.

The presiding officer also reminded the counsels for both parties, as well as senator-judges, that while they may rigorously examine witnesses and test the credibility of their testimonies, they “must refrain from resorting to a manner of questioning or to making declarations that elicit fear rather than candor.”
“The Chair therefore respectfully requests our distinguished colleagues, the counsels for the parties, including this representation, to exercise the restraint expected of us,” he said.

“Unlike in inquiries in aid of legislation, an answer of ‘I do not know’ or ‘I do not recall’ may be extremely frustrating. It’s one that we may encounter numerous times in a proceeding such as this. What we can control, however, is how we appreciate and weigh the testimonies and statements delivered before this Court,” he added.

Escudero said that they owe it to the parties, witnesses, and the institution they represent to conduct the proceedings with fairness, dignity and respect, “in spite and despite our frustration and/or disappointment with what the witness may or may not be saying.” — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: ASEAN Summit: Metro Manila road closures, alternate routes, traffic advisories
articles.summary: (Updated) What commuters and travelers need to know for ASEAN Summit

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 11:10am

MANILA, Philippines (Updated Nov. 12; First published Oct. 29, 2026.) — Motorists, commuters and air travelers should prepare for road closures, traffic restrictions and possible flight disruptions as Metro Manila hosts the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in November.
The summit will run from Nov. 16 to 18 at several venues across the capital, primarily the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City.
Security preparations will affect road access around the venue and may also lead to changes in airport operations.
Special non-working days: Nov. 16 to 18

Malacañang has declared Nov. 16 to 18 special non-working days throughout Metro Manila. This is when the ASEAN Leaders Summit will take place. U.S. President Donald Trump is among the leaders expected to attend the meetings.
Under Proclamation 1447, the work suspension is intended to ease traffic congestion and allow authorities to secure areas used by summit participants.
Road restrictions

The Metropolitan Manila Development Authority explained on Wednesday, November 11, that there will be no widespread road closures during the summit, with restrictions limited to designated security zones around the Philippine International Convention Center and Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex in Pasay City.
However, motorists should prepare for temporary traffic stoppages along major thoroughfares whenever convoys carrying foreign leaders and delegations pass through.

MMDA Chairman Romando Artes warned that traffic could be particularly heavy from November 12 to 14 because of convoy rehearsals, traffic simulations, road repairs and adjustments to barriers ahead of the summit.
Access to four streets within the PICC and CCP security exclusion zone is restricted from November 9 to 18, according to the MMDA.
These are:

items: Atang Dela Rama Street
Vicente Sotto Street
Pedro Bukaneg Street
Magdalena Jalandoni Street

blocks.text: Only accredited personnel and vehicles bearing authorized ASEAN stickers will be allowed inside the restricted perimeter. Government vehicles without proper authorization will also be denied entry.
The MMDA said other major roads will remain open, although motorists should expect delays and temporary traffic restrictions during the movement of official convoys.
Authorities have also advised motorists to avoid Macapagal Boulevard, the World Trade Center area, Diokno Boulevard and portions of Roxas Boulevard because of anticipated traffic congestion.
The MMDA said access restrictions around the PICC will be implemented in two phases.
MMDA
Alternate routes and traffic adjustments
The MMDA has designated alternate routes for vehicles traveling near the PICC and CCP Complex.
Southbound motorists traveling along Roxas Boulevard toward Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard may take the following route:

items: Turn right onto EDSA.
Turn right onto Diokno Boulevard.
Turn right onto Macapagal Boulevard.

blocks.text: Northbound motorists traveling along Diokno Boulevard and Macapagal Boulevard toward Roxas Boulevard may take:

items: Turn right onto Seaside Boulevard.
Turn right onto Macapagal Boulevard.
Turn left onto EDSA.
Turn left onto Roxas Boulevard.

blocks.text: The MMDA will also implement a stop-and-go traffic scheme along roads used by official convoys. Traffic will be temporarily halted when heads of state and their delegations pass, then allowed to resume afterward.
Artes said these interruptions would generally last only a few minutes.
Truck operators will also be required to follow designated routes from Nov. 15 to 18 to keep container trucks away from Roxas Boulevard.
The alternative truck routes cover roads connecting Manila's Port Area, North Harbor, North Diversion Road and President Osmeña Highway.
EDSA bus lanes, number coding
Designated EDSA bus lanes will be shared with official summit convoys to facilitate the movement of foreign delegates.

The Department of Transportation said buses will continue using the lanes, while traffic personnel will manage their movement to accommodate diplomatic convoys. Private motorists may continue using the regular EDSA lanes.
Motorists approaching the Magallanes Flyover from the Ayala Tunnel should also expect temporary traffic stoppages.
Meanwhile, the MMDA has suspended the number coding scheme from Monday, November 16, to Wednesday, November 18.
The MMDA said it will deploy 2,637 personnel to assist with traffic management and security operations, including emergency response teams and towing personnel.
Motorists and commuters are advised to allow additional travel time, follow posted traffic instructions and monitor official MMDA advisories for further adjustments.

For air travelers: More than 300 flights scheduled between Nov. 13 and 19 have been affected by cancelations or rescheduling. Read Philstar.com's list of affected flights. — with a report from John Marwin Elao

articles.title: Historic US ocean liner sinks near Florida to become world’s largest artificial reef
articles.summary:
SS United States, which set transatlantic speed record during maiden voyage in 1952, is sunk off coast of Destin

The historic SS United States has reached the end of its journey at sea,…

blocks.text: The historic SS United States has reached the end of its journey at sea, sinking Wednesday off the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will begin a new life underwater as an artificial reef.

The nearly 1,000ft American-made vessel, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, was launched in 1952 and made history by setting a transatlantic speed record during its maiden voyage. The ship carried thousands of passengers across the Atlantic over 17 years of operation before being retired in 1969.

On Wednesday, the ship was deployed at approximately 2.40pm ET, with the sinking process beginning shortly before 5pm. The ship had been hollowed out, with openings cut into its hull to let water in and help it sink upright to the ocean floor. Over the next several hours, the ship gradually filled with water before finally sinking to the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico around 10pm.

It will rest on the seafloor at a depth of approximately 180ft, the ship’s upper decks sitting about 55ft below the surface. As the world’s largest artificial reef, the site is expected to become a popular diving destination for divers around the world.

For years, the SS United States remained docked in Philadelphia, as various owners attempted to save and restore it. However, the rising costs of maintaining the ageing vessel complicated preservation efforts. In 2021, port authorities raised the daily dockage fee to $1,700, a cost the non-profit SS United States Conservancy could no longer afford.

In 2024, Florida’s Okaloosa county purchased the ship for $1m, with plans to transform it into the world’s largest artificial reef. Officials expect the structure to provide a new habitat for a variety of marine life, including red snapper, grouper, amberjack, mackerel and tuna.

Before its sinking, Susan Gibbs, president and co-founder of the conservancy, said: “She’s being reefed and will remain intact and will become a vibrant and dynamic marine habitat, so that, combined with the land-based museum and visitor experience, will honor her history in a deeply moving way.”

Gibbs, whose grandfather, William Francis Gibbs, designed the ship, also reflected on his personal connection to the vessel, saying: “His relationship with the ship was, I would say, a full-bore obsession. He would joke that he loved the SS United States a thousand times more than my grandmother. He would see the ship off every time she set sail for Europe, and be one of the first to greet her on her return.”

articles.summary: The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is focusing on the “second-round effects” of global supply shocks and the risk of eroding public trust as the country faces “a difficult…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 11:07am
Fresh vegetables are displayed at a market in Quezon City on March 4, 2026.
Michael Varcas / The Philippine STAR

MANILA, Philippines — The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas is focusing on the “second-round effects” of global supply shocks and the risk of eroding public trust as the country faces “a difficult combination” of rising inflation and sluggish growth.

The BSP said on Wednesday, November 12, that it is also considering weak aggregate demand as it works to bring inflation down. It added that restoring price stability and purchasing power is crucial to rebuilding public confidence in the central bank and the economy.

"Signs of improvement would include easing inflation, more stable inflation expectations, stronger business and consumer confidence, and a recovery in investment and employment," the central bank said.

Intending to bring inflation back to its 3% target by 2028, the BSP has raised its benchmark interest rate by 125 basis points in 2026 alone, with a "jumbo" 50-basis-point hike implemented in October.
Inflation for the same month was recorded at a three-year high of 7.8%, driven by high energy and transport costs. Economic growth, meanwhile, weakened to 2.1% in the third quarter of 2026.
The BSP will convene for its final Monetary Board meeting on December 17 and release its last monetary policy report on December 23.

articles.title: Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems
articles.summary:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife

The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from…

blocks.text: The vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster.

The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.

blocks.caption: Before and after satellite images of an oil spill off the coast of UAE in October

blocks.text: Ecosystem at risk

The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.

It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.

blocks.caption: Oil washes up on a beach in Umm Al Quwain, UAE, on 24 October. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.

Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.

“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.

“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”
Strikes and spills

Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.

“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.

More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.

Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.

blocks.caption: The Gem No 2 ablaze at sea

blocks.text: Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.

blocks.caption: The Minoan Pioneer off the coast of Muscat, Oman, on 30 October. Photograph: Arnel Hecimovic/The Guardian

blocks.text: Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Before and after images of an oil slick off UAE in October

blocks.text: Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta, two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.

blocks.caption: A satellite image showing an oil slick spreading off the coast of Kharg Island, a key oil export terminal for Iran, in May. Photograph: Copernicus Sentinel data/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.

Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.

According to a Wall Street Journal report, the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.
The damage ahead

In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.
In Oman, divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.

blocks.caption: An oil slick along the southern coast of Qeshm Island, Iran, on 13 August. Photograph: ISNA/AFP/Getty Images
Beaches being closed in UAE after oil spills caused by tanker attacks

blocks.text: But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.

Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”

Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.

A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.

blocks.caption: Workers clean a stretch of beach after oil washed ashore in Sharjah, UAE, 3 November. Photograph: Altaf Qadri/AP

blocks.text: Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.
“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

articles.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
articles.summary: The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".

blocks.text: A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Friday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

articles.summary:
William, 17, was reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla in Victoria’s Gippsland region

blocks.text: A teenage boy has been found alive after disappearing in dense bushland wearing only shorts and work boots nearly a week ago.
Police AirWing found William, 17, whose surname has not been shared, on Thursday morning.
The teenager was reported missing after straying from his camp near Walhalla, 185km east of Melbourne, in Victoria’s Gippsland region last Friday.
He was dropped off by his mother for the weekend to camp with his friend.
It is believed he walked a short distance back to the drop-off location to retrieve further camping equipment.
When he failed to return shortly after, his stepbrother searched the area but found no trace of the teen.
William’s mobile phone, food and water were left behind.
Police said he was last seen near Stoney Creek Road, between Cowwarr and Walhalla on 6 November about 4pm.
On Wednesday, investigators appealed to hunters, campers and landowners to come forward with any information after a hunting camera was found in the search area.
Emergency service workers, including the dog and rescue squad had been searching the dense bushland since last Friday.
