articles.title: Nvidia board reportedly meeting to decide CEO Jensen Huang’s future as chip giant’s share price plunges – follow live
articles.summary:
Huang’s potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4tn chipmaker he co-founded, with Nvidia’s shares sliding about 8% in ​after-hours trading

Nvidia’s shares…

blocks.text: Jensen Huang's future rests in the balance as Nvidia board reportedly meet

Nvidia’s board is meeting to decide whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang, a source familiar with the matter told the Reuters news agency, as the world’s dominant supplier of AI processors grapples with reports of two extramarital affairs involving its longtime ⁠leader.

The reports mark a sharp escalation in a controversy that began with revelations about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence has said was involved in facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.
In a memo to employees on Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and took “full responsibility,” but gave no details about the relationship.
Huang, 63, has ⁠no obvious successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. He also has dozens of direct reports, underscoring the tight control he maintains over the company.

The company’s shares slid about 8% in ​after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal first reported that Nvidia was preparing to oust Huang. ‌Including Wednesday’s after-hours selloff, Nvidia has lost about $600bn ‌in stock market value this week since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman.
Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had ‌an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.
Key events

items: nowHow did we get here?
17m agoNvidia share price plunges 8% in after-hours trade
40m agoJensen Huang's future rests in the balance as Nvidia board reportedly meet

blocks.text: How did we get here?

Reports that Nvidia’s board is weighing Jensen Huang’s future at the company mark a dramatic escalation in events that began last week, when it was revealed that the CEO had been engaged in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy who was involved in facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.
The chip mogul is alleged to have had a relationship with Alice Huang, a businesswoman that US intelligence services suspect of spying for the Chinese government.

US intelligence agencies believe Alice Huang, acting on behalf of Beijing, pushed Jensen Huang to lobby Trump for relaxed export controls on Nvidia’s sales in China, which he has done multiple times publicly. Nvidia said in a statement that neither trade secrets nor US national security had been compromised.

The affair and alleged intelligence operation involving Huang could have far reaching implications for Nvidia and the tech industry, which are already enduring a period of high market volatility. Huang’s leadership of Nvidia, which is deeply financially intertwined with other leading tech companies like OpenAI, has long been viewed as crucial to the company’s success and stability.

blocks.caption: In this image taken from video provided by TVBS, Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei in 2025. Photograph: TVBS/AP

blocks.text: Huang’s defenders framed his affair as a personal lapse in judgment rather than evidence of treachery against the US, which has imposed strict limits on what chips Nvidia can sell to China.

Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching a probe regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
The probe is being overseen by independent directors with outside legal counsel. At the time it was announced, the ​board expressed confidence in Huang.
Donald Trump has said he ​had not discussed the allegations with Huang but voiced support for ​the Nvidia chief, calling him “an honourable guy” who had “done an amazing job for our country.”
Nvidia share price plunges 8% in after-hours trade

Nvidia’s shares plunged in ⁠after-hours trading on news that its board may oust longtime CEO Jensen Huang, with the chipmaker losing about $600bn ‌in stock market value this week since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman.
Shares in Nvidia slid more than 8% after close of trade.
Strategists said investors were still digesting the implications of the midterm ‌elections, which resulted in Democrats taking control of Congress, but also now, the news surrounding Nvidia.

blocks.caption: American flags are displayed on screens on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Jensen Huang “was the one who led the marvelous rise of Nvidia,” said Bruce Zaro, managing director at Granite Wealth Management in Plymouth, Massachusetts. “I guess the question would be, can someone step up if Jensen has to resign or is forced out?“
“It looks bad from every single ⁠angle,” said Jake Dollarhide, chief executive officer at Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma.

“I believe the board ​won’t oust him until they have an all-star, ‌a known entity in ‌the tech sector, to replace him,” said Jake Dollarhide, chief executive officer at Longbow Asset Management in Tulsa, Oklahoma.
double quotation markAt the end of the day, let’s not forget ‌that the Nvidia chip is the centrepiece of the AI story.“
Analysts have suggested that with no obvious successor, the Nvidia board has a difficult decision to make on whether to remove Jensen Huang as CEO.
“Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place,” Gil Luria, head of technology research at DA Davidson, said.

Huang’s potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4tn chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the top supplier of AI chips at the center of the global artificial-intelligence boom and US-China technology rivalry.
Investors and analysts said while demand for Nvidia’s chips would be unlikely to drop in ​the near term, the broader universe of companies backed by the company might suffer.
“Nvidia is also at the centre of the circular financing which is providing capital to the investment boom,” said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management in Singapore.
double quotation markThey are financing their customers. In these types of booms or bubbles, sometimes all it takes is a slowdown to shift it into the bust phase.”

articles.title: Hegseth, wife and aides spark scolding from guard at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
articles.summary: A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a…

image.caption: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, his wife, Jennifer, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff General Dan Caine attend a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va., on Wednesday. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery issued a verbal reprimand to a group of advisers and staffers with U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth following a Veterans Day ceremony.
Pentagon spokesman said U.S. army sentinel 'correctly and respectfully' called for proper decorum
Video shows Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.
As the group broke from taking photos, a loud laugh could be heard, and the soldier guarding the tomb shouted that "all visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesman, said that "while commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured — and will always honour — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe," he added.
Hegseth delegation appears to be rebuked at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
Incident follows near impeachment of Hegseth

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock — rain or shine — by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.
Hegseth and his staff were at the tomb as part of a larger ceremony commemorating Veterans Day that also was attended by U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice-President JD Vance.
The incident comes a day after Hegseth narrowly survived an effort to impeach him by lawmakers in Congress.

The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, and backed by Democrats. However, while Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed efforts to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.
Hegseth slammed the effort Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the Constitution for his removal.
Republicans block impeachment push against Hegseth

A core part of his argument included the assertion that criticisms of him and his handling of the U.S. military were tantamount to an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.
"On the eve of Veterans Day, these resolutions tell every one of them that their service was a crime," Hegseth said Tuesday.
"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."
Following the reprimand at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, the reaction from Democrats was swift.
Rep. Gwen Moore said Hegseth demonstrated "his utter lack of fitness for his office."

"One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier," she wrote in a social media post.

Pete Hegseth continues to demonstrate his utter lack of fitness for his office. One day after narrowly avoiding impeachment, he shows his contempt for our men and women in uniform by disrespecting the sanctity of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.—RepGwenMoore
It was not the first time members of Trump's team have caused controversy at Arlington National Cemetery.

During his campaign for a second term, Trump attended a ceremony in 2024 to honour U.S. forces killed in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. A campaign staffer reportedly shoved a cemetery employee trying to prevent two people from filming and photographing the event.
U.S. army confirms Arlington cemetery worker 'pushed aside' by Trump staff

Trump, who had been invited by troops' families, later shared a video on TikTok showing him at the cemetery with a voiceover blaming the Biden administration for the "disaster" of the Afghanistan withdrawal.
U.S. law prohibits campaign or election-related activities within national military cemeteries.

articles.title: Series of storms leaves B.C. woman with tree stuck on her house for days
articles.summary: As B.C. continues to batten down its hatches amid the third in a series of major fall storms, one resident who saw a tree fall onto her house last Friday says it'll have to remain in place as high…

image.caption: Olivia Power's house in Prince George saw a tree fall on it last Friday, and it has had to stay in place for multiple days as a series of consecutive storms has made cleanup challenging throughout B.C. (Submitted by Olivia Power)

blocks.text: British Columbia

As B.C. continues to batten down its hatches amid the third in a series of major fall storms, one resident who saw a tree fall onto her house last Friday says it'll have to remain in place as high winds continue to batter the province.
Trees falling on power lines lead to some people to lose power for multiple days throughout B.C.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) has posted a swath of weather warnings throughout B.C., warning of high winds and rainfall, with more than 250 millimetres of rain possible locally on Vancouver Island.
In the Central Interior and Prince George area, thousands have remained without power for multiple days, as B.C. Hydro says the ongoing series of storms has made cleanup challenging.
Prince George resident Olivia Power lost power for three days, from last Friday to Sunday, due to one of the windstorms — which toppled a tree onto her house.
"We couldn't really go outside to look at what had happened. We were just worried with the windstorm that more trees were going to fall down," she said.

Power and her husband went into a basement hallway after the tree fell onto her house last Friday, not wanting to stay near windows as winds picked up. She said there is no water damage currently due to the fallen tree. (Submitted by Olivia Power)
Power said that a tree removal service she called wasn't available until Wednesday at the earliest — but with winds picking up again, the tree would have to stay in place until at least Thursday.
ECCC said in an orange wind warning on Wednesday that winds could gust up to 90 km/h in the Prince George region.

items: Impact of Prince George windstorm still being felt, homeowners face long waits to get trees removed
Flooding prompts evacuation order for part of Pemberton as storm batters B.C.

blocks.text: B.C. Hydro said in an update for the Central Interior that crews were having trouble accessing areas due to fallen trees and debris.
"Additional contractors, specialized equipment and resources have been brought into the region to support restoration efforts," the utility wrote.

#BCStorm update: Crews have made significant progress restoring power in the Central Interior, with most main electrical lines in and around #CityofPG now restored. More than 180 workers continue restoration efforts around the clock as crews focus on remaining outages and areas with significant damage. Strong winds are expected through late afternoon and early evening and may cause additional outages. Stay back at least 10 metres from downed power lines and call 9-1-1 immediately. Read our latest operational update: https://t.co/MoKGIMYFbp—bchydro
Power said that she spoke to some neighbours who told her the windstorms that struck Prince George and the Interior were unprecedented in nature.
"The community has really come together though," she said.

"It's been really nice to see a lot of people wanting to help clear trees and and whatnot, so it's nice knowing that the community got each other's back. Even if we do get hit by another strong storm."
Rainstorm causes Sea-to-Sky Highway rockslide, traffic delays
Luke Lamplugh, who runs Prince George Property Cleanup, said the winds were so high last week that garbage from a nearby dump flew into trees and roof shingles fell into ditches.
He said he hauled over 1,300 kilograms of tree branches to the dump after the first storm hit Prince George late last week, and had some advice for residents as they continue to deal with high winds.
"If you're on natural gas [heating], and the fans don't work because the power is out, then you need to keep your windows closed and try and retain heat in the house," he said.
"That's really important for a lot of folks, especially seniors around here."
Lamplugh also advised residents to store jugs of water in their freezer in case they lose power for multiple days.
With files from Cory Correia and As It Happens

articles.title: Nigeria's president launches re-election manifesto but can he regain voters' trust?
articles.summary: For Nigerians to feel meaningful improvements, reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined, analysts say.

blocks.text: Nigeria's President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has launched his re-election manifesto, promising to grow the economy, tackle insecurity and address housing shortages.
The plan targets 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 78,000 additional security personnel and 200,000 affordable homes.
Titled From Reform to Prosperity, the manifesto builds on Tinubu's first-term economic reforms, including the removal of the fuel subsidy, which has pushed up living costs.
Nigeria is due to hold a general election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar among Tinubu's main challengers.
The manifesto, launched on 10 November by his party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), reflects the government's bid to win back the trust of Nigerians.

Elected in 2023, Tinubu undertook a series of economic reforms, including the removal of fuel subsidies, the harmonisation of official and parallel foreign exchange rates, and tax reforms in Africa's largest oil producer.

"That manifesto was trying to get Nigeria back on its feet, given the condition of the country at that time, slipping into austerity," Joshua Osiyemi, who heads Tracka, a platform launched by the BudgIT Foundation, which is a non-profit organisation that aims to make government financial data easier to understand.
The reforms, although considered necessary by some economists, have been painful for many Nigerians.
"Fuel prices went up, and everything that Nigerians consume skyrocketed," Osiyemi told the BBC.
"Most Nigerian families are saying they cannot survive on 10,000 naira [$7.40; £5.50] a day," he said, referring to a survey conducted by his organisation.

Analysis by Nigeria's International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) found that the price of imported rice rose by 184% between May 2023, when Tinubu took office, and October 2025. Other staples, including beans, garri (cassava flour) and bread, also recorded substantial increases.

In a sign that the reforms might be starting to pay off, SBM Intelligence, a security risk consulting firm, found that the cost of preparing a pot of jollof rice fell by 11.5% between June and September 2026, the sharpest decline it had recorded in the 10 years it has been running its Jollof Index.
However, this has not translated into significant relief for most households.
"Nigerians spend more and more of their income on basics," said Ikenna Okonkwo, head of research at SBM Intelligence.
The reforms were praised by the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for their effectiveness.

Nigeria's headline inflation stood at 14% in September 2026, according to the National Bureau of Statistics, down from a high of 34% in 2024. The gap between the official and parallel exchange rates has also narrowed.
Tinubu has said the removal of fuel subsidies freed up more than one trillion ($740m; £550m) naira in government resources in just the first two months.
However, he has recently said he will work to reduce fuel cost.
His administration subsequently announced a 125bn naira intervention package for small businesses, including grants for smaller enterprises and loans for manufacturers.
Atiku has criticised Tinubu's decision to remove the fuel subsidy.
"My position stands! I will restore subsidy to make life easier and affordable for Nigerians," Atiku wrote on X.
However, restoring the fuel subsidy could prove challenging given Nigeria's economic realities.

"The current budget for Nigeria in 2026 is about 68.32tn naira, with 15.8tn going towards debt servicing. So, we are not fiscally strong enough to say that we want to return to the subsidy," Osiyemi said.
While Tinubu's reforms are lauded for restoring some stability at the macroeconomic level, they have also created instability in households.
Two months away from elections, the cost of living and economic hardship are the major issues for many voters.
"These kinds of things can get punished in polls," said Okonkwo of SBM Intelligence.

To address this, Tinubu promised to lower the cost of living, grow the economy by 6% and halve youth unemployment if he wins re-election. Achieving these targets will require increased oil and agricultural production.
But much of Nigeria's agricultural production is concentrated in the north, where insecurity has made farming increasingly difficult.
Osiyemi says many farmers are reluctant to return to their fields.
"They're not sure whether when they go to their farms, they have the chances of also coming back home, to meet with their family."
To address insecurity, Tinubu proposes recruiting an additional 28,000 military personnel and 50,000 police officers.
"The security situation, especially in the north, is more complex than a matter of just recruiting more soldiers," Okonkwo said.
The threats include jihadists, kidnap gangs and conflict between herders and farmers in central Nigeria.

Insecurity is also a major priority for Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) presidential candidate, who came third in the 2023 presidential election and attracted significant support from young Nigerians.
He unveiled his 2027 Governance Agenda on 10 November, under the campaign slogan "A New Nigeria is Possible", placing national unity at the top of his priorities, followed by security.
"Nobody will kidnap school children and disappear into the bush. If you kidnap children and go into the bush, you will not be alone there. We will come after you," he said.

Further, delivering on those ambitions will also depend on improving electricity supply, particularly for businesses and industries. Tinubu promises to increase available electricity generation towards 10,000MW.
"There is nothing in the manifesto about where that investment is going to come from because it will cost a lot of money," said Okonkwo.

Nigeria's power sector has suffered from years of underinvestment. The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission says the country had installed generation capacity of 13,625MW at the end of 2024, but generated an average of just 4,223MW during the year.
Nigeria's power sector has failed to produce at capacity due to ageing infrastructure, inadequate maintenance, gas supply constraints and funding challenges.

The government has also privatised electricity distribution, but distribution companies have struggled to invest in infrastructure, including local transformers and metering systems, partly because of low profit margins.

"The government cannot increase tariffs to an extent where people will revolt, and that also keeps investors away because they don't look at the Nigerian power sector as somewhere that they can make money," said Okonkwo.
Unreliable electricity supplies force many households and businesses to rely on generators, pushing up the cost of living and doing business.

The manifesto also promises to build 200,000 affordable homes. This is a fraction of Nigeria's estimated housing deficit, which a technical committee set up by the housing ministry put at 14.9 million units in 2025.
For Nigerians to feel a meaningful improvement in their lives, the reforms will need to go beyond the promises outlined in the manifesto, analysts say.
"Some of the items in the manifesto seem bloated, but if they can be committed to it, I want to believe that quite a number of these items that they have here are very much achievable," Osiyemi said.
"The big thing, if the APC wins, which they have to do and is a tall order, is to regain the trust of Nigerians," Okonkwo said.

Nigeria's 2023 presidential election saw Tinubu declared winner with 8.79 million votes, ahead of Atiku and Obi. Tinubu's victory came amid growing economic hardship after eight years of Muhammadu Buhari's APC government.

"APC were able to win because opposition was divided between two very strong candidates with two regional bases. In the end, we still go down to basic questions like the region you are from and tribal sentiments," Okonkwo said.

As Nigeria heads towards the 2027 elections, Tinubu, Atiku and Obi are once again central to the contest, but the opposition faces a familiar challenge: building a united front and support beyond regional strongholds.
"It will play out like it did in 2023," Okonkwo said.
"The APC are in a stronger position being the incumbent party and the momentum that some of the opposition candidates had in 2023 has faded."

articles.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon admits throwing Jesse Baird’s phone off a bridge after alleged murders, trial hears
articles.summary:
Court hears former police officer agrees he was trying to destroy evidence that might incriminate him

Beau Lamarre-Condon has admitted he threw Jesse Baird’s phone off a bridge to destroy…

blocks.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon has admitted he threw Jesse Baird’s phone off a bridge to destroy evidence after allegedly murdering him, a court has heard.
The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
Sitting in the witness box for a sixth day, Lamarre-Condon was asked what he did with Baird’s phone after the alleged murders.
He told the court on Thursday it was thrown off Tom Uglys Bridge near the Shire in Sydney’s south.
“I didn’t want to have any evidence of Jesse’s phone on me… I did throw it off the bridge,” Lamarre-Condon told the New South Wales supreme court.
As part of his cross examination, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC put to him: “you did [that to] destroy evidence on Jesse’s phone that might incriminate you”.
Lamarre-Condon responded: “Essentially, yes”.
The former officer did not deny he had contacted his friend Stacey Parker, who lived in Western Australia, and asked if he could send her the phone for her to throw into a body of water.
But he did not end up mailing her the device.
Lamarre-Condon was also asked by Hatfield if he deleted messages between himself and Baird, alongside photos of them together, after his arrest.
“You did that deliberately to remove evidence of your relationship with Jesse Baird,” Hatfield told the court.
Lamarre-Condon said he disagreed and did not believe he had deleted the messages.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

articles.title: Brooklyn building collapse kills at least one, traps others in wreckage
articles.summary:
Three-story building was at the edge of a construction site where another edifice had been demolished

Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in

blocks.text: Firefighters dug through the rubble of a three-story building in Brooklyn on Wednesday after it collapsed at the edge of a construction site, killing at least one person and trapping others beneath the wreckage.

Firefighters were called to the scene in the borough’s Flatbush section at about 4pm. News helicopter footage showed dozens of firefighters scouring the debris, with a group homing in on one area and appearing to use a saw to cut through the wreckage.
One person died, and four others were rushed to a hospital in critical condition, according to the New York City fire department. Six additional people were taken to hospitals with minor injuries.
The aerial videos showed firefighters digging at least one person out of the rubble and removing them on a stretcher.

blocks.caption: An apartment is exposed after the building collapse in Brooklyn, New York City, on 11 November 2026. Photograph: Kena Betancur/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The building that collapsed had been perched at the edge of a lot where another one-story building had been torn down for a construction project. The site was being excavated, and the building that fell down filled the construction pit with bricks and wood.
Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing.

A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used rescue dogs to search for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they were working.
Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, property owner and general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project.

articles.title: Bronze leg found in Scottish bog sheds new light on Roman occupation
articles.summary:
Once thought to have been looted by Scottish tribes, the gilded limb is the centrepiece of a new exhibition on Roman Scotland in Edinburgh

A large bronze leg found in a bog in rural Scotland…

blocks.text: A large bronze leg found in a bog in rural Scotland more than 200 years ago and then hidden away in a duke’s storeroom is helping to rewrite the history of the Roman empire.

Antiquarians argued that the so-called Mislington leg had been looted, perhaps from York, hacked off by marauding Scottish tribes and carried north over Hadrian’s Wall. “We cannot visualise the conditions which would have led to its erection anywhere north of the Great Wall,” said one scholar, James Curle, in 1932.

But archaeologists now believe the hefty gilded bronze limb came from the Scottish Borders and was part of a vast statue of the emperor Antoninus Pius on horseback, erected near Hawick after his armies had wrested control of southern Scotland in about AD140.

blocks.caption: A marble bust of the emperor Antoninus Pius, during whose reign the Romans occupied parts of Scotland from AD142 to 165. Photograph: World History Archive/Alamy

blocks.text: Bearing significant similarities to imperial statues in other frontier regions, it is the centrepiece of the largest exhibition ever staged on the Romans in Scotland, which opens on Saturday at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh.
It had languished for 100 years in the “charter room” at Dalkeith House near Edinburgh, one of the stately homes owned by the Duke of Buccleuch, after being dug up in 1820.

It is now displayed alongside other artefacts that the museum’s curators believe prove the Romans were a far more significant force north of Hadrian’s Wall than previously realised, occupying large areas of the country, producing new artworks and shaping the politics of Scotland long after they retreated.

Dr Fraser Hunter, the principal curator of the exhibition, Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire, believes such statues would have had a profound impact on iron-age communities. And instead of being hacked off, the leg was carefully removed and deposited where it was found 1,700 years later.

“These kind of things are not only visually dominant but they look really, really alien,” Hunter said. “There is effectively no naturalist art in the iron age – very, very little. The whole idea of depicting a person is absolutely alien to the iron-age worldview.”

Among a series of firsts, the exhibition also includes a new reconstruction of a heavily decorated earthenware bowl from Inveresk, east of Edinburgh. The village is the site of a large Roman fort and town that was, Hunter believes, a centre of imperial power during the Antonine period in Scotland of AD142 to 165 – the second of three periods of Roman occupation of Scotland.

Hunter estimates that about 10,000 troops, including auxiliaries from places such as modern-day Romania and north Africa, were stationed across southern and eastern Scotland, alongside perhaps another 10,000 camp followers, wives and enslaved people.

Bethany Simpson, an assistant curator, said the bowl displayed a unique combination of animal reliefs involving dolphins, stags and a stylised hunting dog. “You only find it in Inveresk. It’s not seen anywhere else in Scotland; it’s not seen anywhere in the UK,” she said.

blocks.caption: Bethany Simpson, an assistant curator, with the ancient bronze leg. Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA

blocks.text: The museum is also showing for the first time two remarkably well preserved, locally carved stone altars from a mithraeum excavated at Inveresk. The museum uses dramatic lighting to demonstrate the vibrant colours originally painted on them.

One has slits cut into its hollowed-out stone, radiating from the carved head of Mithras, with holes carved into its eyes and mouth to allow lamplight to shine out in the smoky darkness of the temple.

blocks.caption: The two spectacular altars from the Roman fort Inveresk’s mithraeum (a temple to the god Mithras).  Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: The show also includes the entire skeleton of a horse, carefully buried at Inveresk, which was also home to a small amphitheatre – a rare find in frontier towns. “The burial of cavalry horses in Britain is rare,” Hunter said. “Normally they just get disposed of, so this must have been a valued steed, which is really interesting.”

The exhibition focuses on Rome’s influence on indigenous Celtic tribes, their culture and political structures. Recent scholarship suggests there was no tradition of carving in pre-Roman Scotland, but from the Roman occupation sprang rich native styles, leading to highly ornate Pictish standing stones.

Celtic rulers were beguiled by the silver used by the Romans for coins and jewellery; until then silver was unknown locally. The Romans used it to buy loyalty. Yet, by the third and fourth centuries, the Roman threat led the Pictish tribes to merge forces into an “anti-Roman coalition”.
“What Roman interventions effectively do is they create a worse enemy. It’s the problem that empires often have in dabbling around their edges,” Hunter said.

“So you get these larger-scale polities emerging. But they are also using Rome as a model, and the emergence of things like the Pictish symbols is absolutely tied into their exposure to sculpture and writing. So these are local responses to these kind of things, but in a highly creative, wonderfully magnificent manner.”

articles.title: Facial recognition errors put ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest, police watchdog warns
articles.summary:
Inspectors find some officers acted on potential matches from retrospective searches without making enough checks

Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic…
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
Although the technology can help fight crime, the report found it is beset by errors and biases, and operators do not always realise they must make further inquiries to verify the data.

The report by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary, published on Wednesday, covers only retrospective facial recognition. The technology is seen as less controversial and less tricky to get right than live facial recognition, which is used in real time to find suspects.
“Some investigators didn’t know that RFR results were intelligence rather than evidence and required further enquiries before officers took enforcement action,” the report said.
“This creates a risk that people could be incorrectly identified or arrested, which could undermine public confidence in the technology.

“We found that some investigators didn’t always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches. In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.”
The report said there are still issues with bias in the algorithm, including being more likely to wrongly flag people from ethnic minorities as suspects.

It said: “More needs to be done to reduce the risks of people being wrongly arrested … Auditors also identified cases where users uploaded poor-quality or unsuitable probe images, including blurred images and images containing multiple faces. These factors reduced the system’s ability to return reliable matches.”
Inspectors also found a risk of public confidence being undermined because custody images that should have been deleted were in fact kept.

The report says: “Inspectors found that legislation hasn’t kept up with changes in facial recognition technology and there is no comprehensive statutory framework governing this technology’s use. This makes it more difficult for forces to understand the lawful basis for RFR’s use and what safeguards are needed to protect the public.”

His Majesty’s Inspector of Constabulary Kathryn Stone said continued public support relied on showing the technology was being used properly: “Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment. A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence.”
Facial recognition is seen by police chiefs as the next big leap forward in crime fighting, and next huge threat to civil liberties by sceptics.
Jasleen Chaggar, from Big Brother Watch, said: “The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming.
after newsletter promotion

“This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they’ve never visited, as we’ve seen before.

“Worse still, police aren’t even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without even realising why they’ve been accused.

“Police cannot be allowed to continue using the algorithm with so few safeguards and at biased settings that are more likely to misidentify women, Asian and black people and search against millions of unlawfully held custody images.”

Ben Russell, lead on facial recognition for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, said: “Policing remains committed to the ethical, proportionate and responsible use of retrospective facial recognition to help investigate crime, bring offenders to justice and keep communities safe and we are pleased that HMICFRS has recognised the exciting possibilities of this technology.”

Prof Pete Fussey of the University of Southampton, formerly a police adviser on facial recognition, said: “Meaningful human scrutiny of AI systems is a legal requirement, yet the report gives examples of investigators taking the computer’s suggestions at face value without further checks.”

articles.title: Nvidia board reportedly weighs ousting Huang amid alleged affairs with exec and suspected Chinese spy

image.caption: Huang's potential ouster would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4 trillion chipmaker he cofounded Image: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nvidia's board prepared to oust co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang and could meet imminently to decide his future, media outlets, led by the Wall Street Journal, reported on Wednesday.
Huang has led the company for more than three decades, turning it from a gaming chipmaker into the dominant supplier of chips for artificial intelligence.
Why is Nvidia's board considering replacing Huang?

The report comes as Nvidia investigates whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after reports of an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.
News that Nvidia might part ways with Huang sent the company's shares down about 8% in after-hours trading.

A reporter for the financial news outlet Bloomberg said on X that Nvidia's board was working with an outside firm to identify potential successors and considering an interim CEO while it searched for a permanent replacement.

articles.title: Mississippi Senate race: Democrat Scott Colom defeats Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith
articles.summary: The southern US state of Mississippi has elected its first Black senator in more than 140 years. Democrat Scott Colom has won the seat in a historic upset, according to projections.

image.caption: The Associated Press projected Colom would defeat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith after more than a week of vote counting (FILE: 03/11/2026)Image: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Democratic candidate Scott Colom beat Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi's US Senate race after a prolonged ballot-counting process, the Associated Press projected on Wednesday.
The narrow victory makes Colom, 43, the state's first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction and the first Democratic senator chosen by Mississippi since 1947.
How Colom pulled ahead in Mississippi
During the campaign, Colom promised to represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society.

"It's got to be about having a party that represents rural America again, suburban America, urban America — a party that makes sure we actually deliver for voters in ways that make their lives better," he said.
The southern US state of Mississippi has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations.
Democrats extend their Senate majority

The Mississippi victory gives the Democrats a 55-44 advantage in the 100-member ​Senate. The winner of the Senate race in Alaska remains to be determined. The Democrats also won control of the House of Representatives, having gained 41 seats so far and holding a 254-to-168 advantage, with 13 races yet to be called.
What will Democrats do with their midterm mandate?

Mississippi election officials have been counting ballots for over a week in a race so close that Colom led by only a few dozen votes at some points. The latest media-tabulated results showed him ahead by more than 4,500 votes, or 0.5 ​percentage points.

The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party suffered defeats in several states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the US South.
Republican rival concedes after close count

Hyde-Smith, 67, posted a concession video on social media, and a spokesperson confirmed she had called Colom to concede. Hyde-Smith was first elected in 2018 and consistently led in opinion polls in a state that ⁠Trump ​won by nearly 23 points in 2024.
Progress or not? Democrats, Republicans pick new leaders in Congress
The Democrats' Senate leader, Chuck Schumer, wrote on X, "Blue Mississippi is here."

Hyde-Smith had blocked Colom's nomination by former President Joe Biden to serve as a US District Court judge in northern Mississippi, citing his position on transgender issues. Mississippi's other US senator, Republican Roger Wicker, supported his nomination for the post.
Mississippi does not have a law mandating a recount for a close election.

MANILA, Philippines — The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte resumes Thursday, November 12, with the defense set to present a representative from the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) as its sole bank witness.

Defense counsel Michael Poa said the defense would no longer present the testimonies of the other bank representatives it initially listed as intended witnesses, citing time constraints and the need to shorten the proceedings.
Lawyer Paul Roderick Ysmael, BPI senior vice president, is the only bank representative who will be presented by the defense out of the 16 initially included in its witness list.
The bank representatives were among the witnesses identified by Duterte's defense team in connection with its presentation of evidence.
The impeachment trial is currently discussing Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, which concerns alleged unexplained wealth and failure to properly declare assets.

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate race in surprise victory for party
articles.summary: Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.

blocks.text: Democrat Scott Colom has won the US Senate race in Mississippi, delivering a shock victory for the party in a deeply conservative state that has elected Republicans for decades.
Colom's victory makes him the first black person from Mississippi to be elected to the US Senate in more than 140 years.
Only a few thousand votes separated Colom from his Republican opponent, the incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The margin was so close that the race could not be called until more than a week after election day, as local officials counted every single ballot that had arrived before the deadline.
Colon won with 49.2% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith received 48.7% and an independent candidate got 2.1%, according to figures from CBS.
The result means the Democratic majority in the Senate is now 55 seats, with a knife-edge race in Alaska still to be called.
It also wipes away a Republican winning streak in Mississippi that dates back to 1982.
The Mississippi contest was never expected to be this close, with Hyde-Smith running for re-election in a state that President Donald Trump won in the 2024 election by more than 22 points.
But Democrats have scored a series of major wins in these midterm elections as the party won control of both the House and the Senate.
It has won Senate seats in numerous Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas.
Polls suggest this was due in large part to voter frustrations with the economy and the Iran war under President Trump.

articles.title: Russian Foreign Ministry says its ambassador to US has died
articles.summary: Russia's Foreign Ministry has said that Alexander Darchiev died from a chronic illness at the age of 66. The long-time diplomat had been in the Washington post since early 2025.

image.caption: Alexander Darchiev was appointed ambassador to the US after Donald Trump returned to the White HouseImage: Russian Foreign Ministry/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia's Foreign Ministry said Wednesday that Alexander Darchiev, Moscow's ambassador to the US, died from an unspecified chronic illness in Moscow at the age of 66.

Darchiev was appointed to the post by Russian President Vladimir Putin in March 2025 after Donald Trump returned to the White House and the two countries sought to improve relations. The post had been vacant for six months before his appointment after hardliner Anatoly Antonov was relieved of his duties in October 2024.

In a statement, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described Darchiev as "an outstanding diplomat, experienced leader, good comrade and mentor" and a brilliant scholar on US history and affairs.
What was Russia's ambassador to US known for?
Zakharova warned against the spread of conspiracy theories surrounding Darchiev's passing, accusing US media outlets of being "particularly active" in that regard.
Darchiev, known for his public denunciations of the West, had previously led the Foreign Ministry's North America and North Atlantic departments and served as ambassador to Canada from 2014 to 2021.
He also led Russia's negotiating team during February 2025 Ukraine peace talks with the US in Istanbul, Turkey.
No date has been given for his funeral.
Details for a memorial service will be announced at a later date, Zakharova said.

articles.summary: Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom will be the state's first Black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom's victory also offers Democrats an unexpected boost in their effort to win…

image.caption: Mississippi Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom, seen at his campaign headquarters in Jackson, Miss., on Wednesday, where he delivered the party a major upset in its efforts to take control of the Senate. (Ellen Schmidt/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom will be the state's first Black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. Colom's victory also offers Democrats an unexpected boost in their effort to win control of the Senate.
Colom will be state's first Black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era
Democrat Scott Colom won election Wednesday to the U.S. Senate representing Mississippi, defeating Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Colom will be Mississippi's first Black senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. His victory also offers Democrats an unexpected boost in their effort to win control of the Senate.

A local prosecutor, he waged an aggressive campaign to take advantage of a tough national environment for Republicans and the fact that Mississippi has a larger share of Black voters than any other state.
Hyde-Smith, a staunch ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, was trying to win her second full term. She was first appointed to fill a vacancy and then won a 2018 special election.
The Associated Press declared Colom the winner at 5:58 p.m. ET.

articles.title: Martin Luther King Jr.'s handwritten draft of 'I Have a Dream' speech found in desk drawer
articles.summary: The day Martin Luther King Jr. stood on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial and delivered his iconic "I Have A Dream" speech is forever etched in the annals of history. But the night before — when the…

image.caption: U.S. civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. waves to supporters during the Aug. 28, 1963, March on Washington, where he delivered his famous 'I Have a Dream' speech. (AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: The day Martin Luther King Jr. stood on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., and delivered his iconic "I Have A Dream" speech to an uproarious crowd is forever etched in the annals of history.
But the night before — when the U.S. civil rights leader stayed up alone in his hotel room scribbling his now-famous words on a yellow notepad — was a moment lost to time. Until now.
King's handwritten final draft of his Aug. 28, 1963, speech has been unearthed from a desk drawer and made public for the first time in six decades.
Lerone Martin, one of the scholars who reviewed the discovery, said looking at those pen-scratched pages sent him travelling back in time.

"It really puts you in the moment, almost puts you into the room with him as he's wrestling with these ideas and preparing to make what he knows will be one of the biggest speeches of his life," Martin, director of Stanford University's Martin Luther King Jr. Research and Education Institute, told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
LISTEN | Interview with MLK scholar Lerone Martin:
As It Happens6:42Only hand-written final draft of Martin Luther King Jr's 'I Have a Dream' speech going up for auction

The seven-page document is the only known copy of King's final draft of the speech before he sent it to be typed the following morning and read it almost verbatim during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.
It will be on display in Atlanta, Chicago and New York City before being put up for auction on Jan. 22, 2027, when it is expected to fetch upwards of $10 million US ($14 million Cdn).
The proceeds will be distributed to several charities, including the King Center in Atlanta, which King founded with his wife, Coretta Scott King.
Found in desk drawer of longtime aide

Xernona Clayton, a broadcaster and civil rights activist, said she first came upon the draft in the 1990s in the desk drawer of her late husband, Edward T. Clayton, King's longtime aide and speechwriter.
At the time, she left it where she found it.

Clayton, who was close friends with King and Coretta Scott, told the New York Times that, for many years, she refused to sell any of her King memorabilia for fear of disrespecting a man she "loved a lot."
Civil rights activist Xernona Clayton found the draft in her late husband's desk drawer. (Scripps/Getty Images)
"Now that I'm older, I’m wiser, and it just seems like something that important ought to be shared," the 96-year-old said.
She's auctioning the draft on behalf of the Still Marching Irrevocable Charitable Unitrust, which she founded and which will distribute the proceeds to several charities.
Clayton did not respond to CBC's requests for comment.
'I could not believe what I was looking at'
When Peter Klarnet, a manuscripts specialist at Christie's auction house in New York, first laid eyes on the pages of King's historic speech, he said he was in "a state of utter disbelief."
"I could not believe what I was looking at," he told CBC.

In his 30 years of working with manuscripts, Klarnet said, he's handled important letters from physicist Albert Einstein and the U.S. founding fathers — and even a printed draft of the original U.S. Constitution.
But none of it compares to this, he said.
"I have never had the privilege and the honour to handle something so universally important, not just to our nation's history but to world history," Klarnet said.
The pages show King's revisions of his speech that were made late into the night. (Christie's)
Klarnet said King, who was also a Baptist minister, is believed to have started writing the speech on Aug. 24 in collaboration with several of his colleagues, including Clayton.
But the night before the March on Washington, he was still perfecting the prose until 3 or 4 a.m.
The pages show words, or sometimes entire sentences, scratched out in blue pen and rewritten. One page has a small brown smudge, possibly a coffee stain.

"It's a beautiful thing to behold," Martin, the Stanford scholar, said. "To watch someone who is so gifted at their craft, and then you get a peek behind the curtain to actually see how this master goes about their task."
King was a gifted orator but rarely wrote down his words, says one scholar. (Christie's)
While King's spoken words reverberate throughout history, Martin said he "rarely wrote things down."
This draft's mere existence is a testament to how important King knew this speech could be, he said.
But the speech's most famous refrain — "I have a dream" — doesn't appear in the draft.

items: When Martin Luther King Jr. told CBC-TV about the fight for civil rights

blocks.text: That's not surprising, Martin said, as those words are also absent from the typed version that followed.
He said that's because King had already used variations of that theme several times before at rallies in North Carolina, Detroit, and Rochester and Albany, both in New York state.
"As he was preparing the speech and debating with his colleagues, many of them told him to not use that part of the speech," Martin said. "They thought it was trite. They thought it was overdone."
Lerone Martin is director of the Martin Luther King Jr. Research and Education Institute at Stanford University in California. (Luna K.)
But in the heat of the moment, Martin said, the famous orator responded to the audience's energy and pivoted.
At one point during his speech, gospel singer Mahalia Jackson can be heard shouting: "Tell them about the dream, Martin!"
"King said that the audience was in a great spirit, the audience was very enthusiastic and receptive, and so he decided to just insert it and use it," Martin said.
Bound for a private collection?
Martin said King focused his speech on what he believed were the "the three major evils or ills that plagued society": poverty, racism and war.
"He called them the evil triplets because he thought they were all interrelated," Martin said, adding it's a message that still resonates today.

"I'm also thankful that it was discovered right now, at a moment where, in the United States of America, we are wrestling with what it means to keep the American dream alive — and not just for a select few, but for everyone," he said.

items: Trump administration releases flood of FBI records on Martin Luther King Jr.
We're all winging it in life, just like MLK did in his 'I Have a Dream' speech

blocks.text: Martin said he hopes the draft doesn't end up tucked away in a private collection when the auction closes.

"I count this text as part of what we call American scripture," he said. "I would love for this text to end up in a public space where the public will be able to see it, to be able to embrace it and to reflect on it."

articles.title: Secretary of Sport says Canada will not allow Russians to play at world junior championships
articles.summary: Canada's Secretary of Sport says the country will not allow Russian players to compete at the upcoming world junior championships, even if they already hold valid visas.

image.caption: Canada's Secretary of Sport, Adam van Koeverden released a statement Wednesday announcing Canada will not allow Russian players to compete at the upcoming world junior championships, even if they already hold valid visas. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Hockey
Canada's Secretary of Sport says the country will not allow Russian players to compete at the upcoming world junior championships, even if they already hold valid visas.
It was not clear if the decision would put Norway back into tournament

Adam van Koeverden's statement Wednesday comes a week after the Canadian government threatened to supersede the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision to force the International Ice Hockey Federation to allow Russia back by refusing to offer visas for the tournament the country is hosting.

It was not immediately clear if the decision would put Norway back into the tournament for the best men's players under the age of 20 that is set to begin on Dec. 26 in the Canadian province of Alberta. Norway said last weekend it had been informed by the IIHF that it had been bumped from the world juniors to fit Russia, which had been banned since invading Ukraine in early 2022.

"These measures are not directed at the Russian and Belarusian people," van Koeverden said. "Rather, they are intended to prevent the governments of Russia and Belarus from using international sporting events hosted in Canada as platforms for state representation, political legitimacy and propaganda.

items: Canada's secretary of sport questions Russia competing as neutrals at Alberta world juniors
Prime Minister says Russia will not be allowed to compete at 2026 world juniors in Alberta

blocks.text: "Canada's position is unequivocal: As long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual. Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Hockey Canada referred to statements last week when asked again about the latest development. A message sent to the IIHF seeking comment and clarification on the status of the final team in the field between Norway and Russia had not been returned.

articles.title: Donald Trump to join Marcos, ASEAN leaders for Manila summit on Nov. 17
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump is expected to attend the ASEAN-US Special Summit in Manila on November 17, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Wednesday, November 11.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 7:08am
U.S. President Donald Trump greets Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the White House on July 22, 2025 in Washington, DC.
Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images / AFP
MANILA, Philippines — US President Donald Trump is expected to attend the ASEAN-US Special Summit in Manila on November 17, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Wednesday, November 11.

Trump is among the foreign leaders expected to join the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, which the Philippines will host from November 15 to 18 at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will lead the meetings as the Philippines wraps up its year as chair of the regional bloc before handing over the leadership to Singapore.

One of the major issues facing ASEAN is the long-delayed negotiations with China for a South China Sea Code of Conduct, which aims to prevent maritime disputes and incidents from escalating into conflict.
ASEAN had set a 2026 target to conclude the negotiations, but it remains uncertain whether the agreement will be completed before the Philippines ends its chairship.
The summit will open on November 15 with plenary and retreat sessions, where leaders will review the Philippines' priorities and discuss the situation in Myanmar.

Leaders from Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam are expected to attend. Myanmar will be represented by the director general of its Foreign Ministry's ASEAN Affairs Department.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and a representative of the International Monetary Fund will also take part as “Guests of the Chair.”

The Related Summits, or the Plus One Summits, with ASEAN's dialogue partners will be held from November 16 to 17. These will bring together representatives from Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, the United Nations and the United States.

On November 17, Marcos will chair the 29th ASEAN Plus Three Summit with China, Japan and South Korea, as well as the 21st East Asia Summit, which tackles regional strategic, political and economic concerns.
The Philippines is also expected to present the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, a proposed binding regional agreement on digital trade and cooperation.
Marcos will lead the closing ceremony and turn over the ASEAN chairship to Singapore before the ASEAN-US Special Summit, which Trump is expected to attend.
Trump last visited the Philippines in 2017 for the ASEAN Summit during his first term. He is scheduled to travel to China afterward for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen.
His expected visit has drawn opposition from civil society groups, some of which have announced plans to hold protests.
Malacañang has declared November 16 to 18 special non-working days in Metro Manila to help ease traffic and ensure the security of visiting leaders and delegates. — with a report from Cristina Chi

articles.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
articles.summary:
Remains believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians repatriated after being flown back by diplomats

Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.

The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.

Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.

blocks.caption: A wood engraving depicting enslaved people being abused on a Brazilian sugar plantation, English, 1845. Photograph: Granger/Historical Picture Archive/Alamy

blocks.text: The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.

“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.

The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.

“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.

Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.

During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.

blocks.caption: One of the boxes containing a skull, at the National Museum in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Wednesday. Photograph: Ludmila Duarte/MDHC

blocks.text: “It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.

It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.

Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.

Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.

The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.

Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.

“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”
